notes.front: In physics, what is matter?
notes.back: What all things are made of: whatever occupies space, has mass and can be perceived by the senses in some way.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls matter the foundation, or building blocks, of any discussion of physics.
notes.example: Like the fuel in a tank, the air in a tyre and the metal of a wing: liquid, gas or solid, each takes up space.
notes.evidence: Matter is the foundation, or the building blocks, for any discussion of physics. According to the dictionary, matter is what all things are made of; whatever occupies space, has mass, and is perceptible to the senses in some way.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Matter”, p. 5-1

notes.front: What is the density of a substance?
notes.back: Its weight per unit volume, such as pounds per cubic foot.
notes.explanation: To find it, both weight and volume must be known, and the weight is divided by the volume.
notes.example: Like comparing a bucket of sand with a bucket of feathers, but per cubic foot of each.
notes.evidence: To find the density of a substance, its weight and volume must be known. Its weight is then divided by its volume to find the weight per unit volume.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Density”, p. 5-2

notes.front: What is specific gravity?
notes.back: A ratio comparing a substance’s density with a standard: water for liquids and solids, usually air for gases.
notes.explanation: In physics the word “specific” implies a ratio; hydrogen is also sometimes the standard for gases.
notes.example: Like saying a liquid is “eight-tenths as heavy as water” instead of giving its weight per cubic foot.
notes.evidence: Water is the standard that physicists have chosen to use when comparing the densities of all liquids and solids. For gases, air is most commonly used, but hydrogen is also sometimes used as a standard for gases. In physics, the word “specific” implies a ratio.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Specific Gravity”, p. 5-2

notes.front: What is potential energy?
notes.back: Energy at rest, or energy that is stored.
notes.explanation: The handbook sorts it into three groups: energy due to position, to distortion of an elastic body, and to chemical action.
notes.example: Like a book resting on a high shelf: nothing moves yet, but energy is there to be released.
notes.evidence: Potential energy is defined as being energy at rest, or energy that is stored. Potential energy may be classified into three groups: (1) energy due to position, (2) energy due to distortion of an elastic body, and (3) energy which produces work
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Potential Energy”, p. 5-2

notes.front: What is kinetic energy?
notes.back: Energy that is in motion.
notes.explanation: An aeroplane rolling down the runway and a rotating flywheel on an engine are the handbook’s examples.
notes.example: Like a thrown ball, but any moving mass has it, from a taxiing aeroplane to a spinning shaft.
notes.evidence: Kinetic energy is defined as being energy that is in motion. An airplane rolling down the runway or a rotating flywheel on an engine are both examples of kinetic energy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Kinetic Energy”, p. 5-3

notes.front: How does the handbook define force?
notes.back: The intensity of an impetus, or of an input; applied to an object, it tends to make the object move.
notes.explanation: Work, power and torque can only exist if a force initiates the process.
notes.example: Like a push on a hangar door: the push is the force, whether or not the door moves.
notes.evidence: force is the intensity of an impetus, or the intensity of an input. For example, if we apply a force to an object, the tendency will be for the object to move. Another way to look at it is that for work, power, or torque to exist, there must be a force that initiates the process.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Force”, p. 5-4

notes.front: In the mechanical sense, when is work done?
notes.back: When a resistance is overcome by a force acting through a measurable distance.
notes.explanation: Two factors are involved, force and movement through a distance, so both must be present.
notes.example: Like hoisting a toolbox onto a bench: a force moves it through a height.
notes.evidence: Work, in the mechanical sense of the term, is done when a resistance is overcome by force acting through a measurable distance. Two factors are involved: (1) force and (2) movement through a distance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Work”, p. 5-4

notes.front: What three kinds of friction does the handbook classify?
notes.back: Starting (static) friction, sliding friction and rolling friction.
notes.explanation: Once a body is moving, keeping it sliding takes a definitely larger force than keeping it rolling.
notes.example: Like the grip between shoe soles and a hangar floor that lets a person walk at all.
notes.evidence: Also, after a body is in motion, a definitely larger force is required to keep it sliding than to keep it rolling. Thus, the three kinds of friction may be classified as: (1) starting or static friction, (2) sliding friction, and (3) rolling friction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Friction & Work”, p. 5-5

notes.front: What is one horsepower equal to, and where did the figure come from?
notes.back: 550 ft-lb per second, from an average horse lifting 550 lb one foot in one second.
notes.explanation: It came from wanting to know how many horses the new steam engine was equivalent to.
notes.example: Like rating a winch by how many horses it could replace, but in foot-pounds per second.
notes.evidence: People wanted to know how many horses the steam engine was equivalent to. The value we know currently as one horsepower (hp) was developed, and it is equal to 550 footpounds per second (ft-lb/s) because of this. It was found that the average horse could lift a weight of 550 lb, one foot off the ground, in one second.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Power”, p. 5-6

notes.front: How does the handbook describe torque?
notes.back: Force acting along a distance, which creates twisting and tries to make something rotate.
notes.explanation: Work is force acting through a distance; torque is force acting along one.
notes.example: Like the twist a hand puts on a stiff jar lid.
notes.evidence: Whereas work is described as force acting through a distance, torque is described as force acting along a distance. Torque is something that creates twisting
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Torque”, p. 5-6

notes.front: What is mechanical advantage?
notes.back: A comparison of output force to input force, or of output distance to input distance.
notes.explanation: A gain in force always comes with a fractional disadvantage in distance.
notes.example: Like a long pry bar that lets a light push lift a heavy crate, but only a little way.
notes.evidence: mechanical advantage is a comparison of the output force to the input force, or the output distance to the input distance. If there is a mechanical advantage in terms of force, there will be a fractional disadvantage in terms of distance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Mechanical Advantage of Machines”, p. 5-8

notes.front: What are the three basic parts of every lever?
notes.back: A fulcrum, an effort (force) and a resistance.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the lever the simplest machine, and perhaps the most familiar; a seesaw is one.
notes.example: Like a bottle opener prising off a cap: it pivots on the cap’s edge while the hand pushes.
notes.evidence: The simplest machine, and perhaps the most familiar one, is the lever. A seesaw is a familiar example of a lever, with two people sitting on either end of a board and a pivoting point in the middle. There are three basic parts in all levers. They are the fulcrum “F,” a force or effort “E,” and a resistance “R.”
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “The Lever”, p. 5-8

image.alt: Three levers drawn as bars. First class: fulcrum between effort and resistance. Second class: fulcrum at one end, effort at the other end, resistance between them. Third class: fulcrum at one end, resistance at the other end, effort between them.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), chapter 5, “The Lever”

notes.front: What is a pulley?
notes.back: A simple machine: a wheel on a fixed axis supported by a frame, normally grooved for a rope.
notes.explanation: The wheel is also called a sheave, and the frame that supports it is called a block.
notes.example: Like the wheel at the top of a flagpole that the halyard runs over.
notes.evidence: Pulleys are simple machines in the form of a wheel mounted on a fixed axis and supported by a frame. The wheel, or disk, is normally grooved to accommodate a rope. The wheel is sometimes referred to as a “sheave,” or sometimes “sheaf.” The frame that supports the wheel is called a block.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “The Pulley”, p. 5-9

notes.front: How do two meshed gears behave as a machine?
notes.back: Like a first class lever, with one gear driving the other.
notes.explanation: The gear receiving the input force is the drive gear; the other is the driven gear.
notes.example: Like the toothed wheels inside a hand drill, where one turns the other.
notes.evidence: Two gears with teeth on their outer edges, as shown in Figure 5-13, act like a first class lever when one gear drives the other. The gear with the input force is called the drive gear, and the other is called the driven gear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “The Gear”, p. 5-10

notes.front: What is an inclined plane?
notes.back: A simple machine for raising or lowering heavy objects with a small force over a relatively long distance.
notes.explanation: The load is moved with less force, paid for with a longer distance.
notes.example: Like a wheelchair ramp beside a flight of steps.
notes.evidence: The inclined plane is a simple machine that facilitates the raising or lowering of heavy objects by application of a small force over a relatively long distance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Inclined Plane”, p. 5-11

notes.front: What is stress?
notes.back: The reaction that occurs inside an object when an external force is applied to it.
notes.explanation: It is typically measured in pounds per square foot or pounds per square inch.
notes.example: Like the pull carried inside a tow rope when a car is towed.
notes.evidence: Whenever an external force is applied to an object, like a weight pushing on the end of a lever, a reaction will occur inside the object which is known as stress. Stress is typically measured in pounds per square foot or pounds per square inch (psi).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Stress”, p. 5-12

notes.front: When is an object said to be strained?
notes.back: When it becomes distorted by an applied force.
notes.explanation: Matter tends to be elastic: forced out of shape by a force, it returns to its original shape when the force is removed.
notes.example: Like a rubber band stretching as it is pulled.
notes.evidence: One characteristic of matter is that it tends to be elastic, meaning it can be forced out of shape when a force is applied and then return to its original shape when the force is removed. When an object becomes distorted by an applied force, the object is said to be strained.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Strain”, p. 5-14

notes.front: What is acceleration?
notes.back: The rate of change of velocity.
notes.explanation: Any increase in velocity, such as from 20 mph to 30 mph, means the object has been accelerated.
notes.example: Like a car’s speed climbing as the driver presses the pedal.
notes.evidence: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity. If the velocity of an object is increased from 20 mph to 30 mph, the object has been accelerated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Acceleration”, p. 5-15

notes.front: What does Newton’s first law of motion state?
notes.back: Objects at rest tend to stay at rest, and moving objects keep the same speed and direction, unless an external force acts.
notes.explanation: It describes inertia, which the handbook calls a property of matter.
notes.example: Like a coffee cup sliding forward on a dashboard when a car brakes hard.
notes.evidence: Inertia is a property of matter. This property of matter is described by Newton’s first law of motion, which states: Objects at rest tend to remain at rest and objects in motion tend to remain in motion at the same speed and in the same direction, unless acted on by an external force.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Newton’s Law of Motion, First Law”, p. 5-16

notes.front: What does Newton’s second law of motion state, as the handbook puts it?
notes.back: The rate of change of a body’s momentum is proportional to the applied force; hence force = mass × acceleration.
notes.explanation: The handbook derives its formula for thrust from this law.
notes.example: Like needing a harder push to speed up a loaded trolley than an empty one.
notes.evidence: When a force acts upon a body, the momentum of that body is changed. The rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force. Based on Newton’s second law, the formula for calculating thrust is derived, which states that force equals mass times acceleration (F = MA).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Newton’s Law of Motion, Second Law”, p. 5-16

notes.front: What does Newton’s third law of motion state?
notes.back: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
notes.explanation: It is often called the law of action and reaction.
notes.example: Like a skater pushing off a wall and gliding backwards.
notes.evidence: Newton’s third law of motion is often called the law of action and reaction. It states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Newton’s Law of Motion, Third Law”, p. 5-17

notes.front: What is circular motion?
notes.back: The motion of an object along a curved path that has a constant radius.
notes.explanation: The handbook pictures an object tied to a string and swung in a circle by hand.
notes.example: Like a bucket of water swung round on a rope.
notes.evidence: Circular motion is the motion of an object along a curved path that has a constant radius. For example, if one end of a string is tied to an object and the other end is held in the hand, the object can be swung in a circle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Circular Motion”, p. 5-17

notes.front: What is a British thermal unit (BTU)?
notes.back: The heat needed to change the temperature of 1 lb of water by 1 °F.
notes.explanation: It is the unit commonly used for engine thermal efficiencies and the heat content of aviation fuel.
notes.example: Like a calorie, but based on a pound of water and degrees Fahrenheit.
notes.evidence: One BTU is defined as the amount of heat required to change the temperature of 1 lb of water 1 degree Fahrenheit (1 °F). The calorie and the gram are seldom used in discussing aviation maintenance. The BTU, however, is commonly referred to in discussions of engine thermal efficiencies and the heat content of aviation fuel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Heat Energy Units”, p. 5-18

notes.front: What is thermal efficiency?
notes.back: The relationship between the power potential in a heat source and the usable power created from it.
notes.explanation: It is calculated as horsepower produced divided by the potential horsepower in the fuel.
notes.example: Like a mark out of ten for an engine: how much of the fuel’s energy ends up as useful power.
notes.evidence: Thermal efficiency is the relationship between the potential for power contained in a specific heat source, and how much usable power is created when that heat source is used. The formula for calculating thermal efficiency is: Thermal Efficiency = Horsepower Produced ÷ Potential Horsepower in Fuel
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Heat Energy and Thermal Efficiency”, p. 5-19

notes.front: By what three methods is heat transferred?
notes.back: Conduction, convection and radiation.
notes.explanation: Heat may move from one location to another, or from one substance to another.
notes.example: Like warmth passing from a hot mug into cold hands.
notes.evidence: There are three methods by which heat is transferred from one location to another or from one substance to another. These three methods are conduction, convection, and radiation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Heat Transfer”, p. 5-19

notes.front: What is the specific heat of a substance?
notes.back: The ratio of its specific heat capacity to the specific heat capacity of water.
notes.explanation: Being a ratio, it has no units and applies in both the English and metric systems.
notes.example: Like comparing how long a pan of oil takes to warm with the same mass of water.
notes.evidence: The specific heat of a substance is the ratio of its specific heat capacity to the specific heat capacity of water. Specific heat is expressed as a number which, because it is a ratio, has no units and applies to both the English and the metric systems.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Specific Heat”, p. 5-21

notes.front: What is pressure?
notes.back: The amount of force acting on a specific amount of surface area.
notes.explanation: With force in pounds and area in square inches, the units are pounds per square inch (psi).
notes.example: Like a person’s weight spread over snowshoes rather than boot heels.
notes.evidence: Pressure is the amount of force acting on a specific amount of surface area. The force is typically measured in pounds and the surface area in square inches, making the units of pressure pounds per square inch or psi.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Pressure”, p. 5-22

notes.front: What does Boyle’s law state?
notes.back: The volume of an enclosed dry gas varies inversely with its absolute pressure, provided the temperature stays constant.
notes.explanation: In Boyle’s law calculations, pressure must always be absolute.
notes.example: Like a sealed syringe: the smaller the air space, the harder the plunger pushes back.
notes.evidence: Boyle’s law is normally stated: “The volume of an enclosed dry gas varies inversely with its absolute pressure, provided the temperature remains constant.” The following formula is used for Boyle’s law calculations. Remember, pressure needs to be in the absolute.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Boyle’s Law”, p. 5-24

notes.front: What does Charles’ law state?
notes.back: Gases expand and contract in direct proportion to the change in absolute temperature, provided the pressure is held constant.
notes.explanation: It is named after the French scientist Jacques Charles.
notes.example: Like a party balloon shrinking when carried from a warm room into the cold.
notes.evidence: The French scientist, Jacques Charles, provided much of the foundation for the modern kinetic theory of gases. He found that all gases expand and contract in direct proportion to the change in the absolute temperature, provided the pressure is held constant.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Charles’ Law”, p. 5-25

notes.front: What does Dalton’s law state?
notes.back: The pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of their partial pressures.
notes.explanation: The law is credited to Dalton, an English physicist.
notes.example: Like two gases sharing one cylinder, each pushing on the walls as if it were alone.
notes.evidence: The pressure of the mixed gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures. This fact was discovered by Dalton, an English physicist
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Dalton’s Law”, p. 5-26

notes.front: What did Pascal discover about pressure in a fluid?
notes.back: Pressure set up in a fluid acts equally in all directions, at right angles to the containing surfaces.
notes.explanation: The discovery, in 1653, established the foundations of modern hydraulics and pneumatics.
notes.example: Like squeezing a sealed tube of toothpaste: the push is felt all over, not only under the thumb.
notes.evidence: The foundations of modern hydraulics and pneumatics were established in 1653 when Pascal discovered that pressure set up in a fluid acts equally in all directions. This pressure acts at right angles to containing surfaces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Pascal’s Law”, p. 5-27

notes.front: What does Bernoulli’s principle state?
notes.back: A fluid’s static pressure decreases where its velocity increases, provided no energy is added or taken away.
notes.explanation: The air’s velocity is kinetic energy and its static pressure is potential energy.
notes.example: Like water speeding up through a narrowed hose nozzle.
notes.evidence: The static pressure of a fluid, liquid or gas, decreases at points where the velocity of the fluid increases, provided no energy is added to nor taken away from the fluid. The velocity of the air is kinetic energy and the static pressure of the air is potential energy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Bernoulli’s Principle”, p. 5-30

notes.front: What is the Mach number?
notes.back: The ratio of an aircraft’s speed to the speed of sound.
notes.explanation: It honours the Austrian scientist Ernst Mach.
notes.example: Like describing a runner as at “half the record pace”, but the yardstick is the speed of sound.
notes.evidence: The term “Mach number” has been given to the ratio of the speed of an aircraft to the speed of sound, in honor of Ernst Mach, an Austrian scientist.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Mach Number”, p. 5-31

notes.front: What causes atmospheric pressure, and what is it at sea level on a standard day?
notes.back: The weight of the atmosphere; 14.7 psi.
notes.explanation: A 1-in² column of air reaching to the top of the atmosphere weighs 14.7 lb on a standard day.
notes.example: Like the water pressing on a diver, but from a sea of air above us.
notes.evidence: This pressure is due to the weight of the atmosphere. On a standard day at sea level, if a 1-in2 column of air extending to the top of the atmosphere was weighed, it would weigh 14.7 lb. That is why standard day atmospheric pressure is said to be 14.7 pounds per square inch (14.7 psi).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Atmospheric Pressure”, p. 5-34

notes.front: How does atmospheric density change with altitude?
notes.back: It decreases as altitude increases.
notes.explanation: Temperature and pressure both fall with altitude, but pressure drops more rapidly.
notes.example: Like the thin air a climber notices high on a mountain.
notes.evidence: Since both temperature and pressure decrease with altitude, it might appear that the density of the atmosphere would remain fairly constant with increased altitude. This is not true, however, because pressure drops more rapidly with increased altitude than does the temperature. The result is that density decreases with increased altitude.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Atmospheric Density”, p. 5-34

notes.front: What is the dew point?
notes.back: The temperature to which humid air must be cooled, at constant pressure, to become saturated.
notes.explanation: If the temperature drops below it, condensation occurs.
notes.example: Like the moment a can of cold drink starts to “sweat” on a warm day.
notes.evidence: The dew point is the temperature to which humid air must be cooled at constant pressure to become saturated. If the temperature drops below the dew point, condensation occurs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Dew Point”, p. 5-36

notes.front: What is vapour pressure (“vapor pressure” in FAA usage)?
notes.back: The part of atmospheric pressure exerted by the moisture in the air.
notes.explanation: It is expressed in tenths of an inch of mercury and is directly related to the dew point.
notes.example: Like one voice’s share of the noise in a crowded room.
notes.evidence: Vapor pressure is the portion of atmospheric pressure that is exerted by the moisture in the air, which is expressed in tenths of an inch of mercury. The dew point for a given condition depends on the amount of water pressure present; thus, a direct relationship exists between the vapor pressure and the dew point.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Vapor Pressure”, p. 5-36

notes.front: What is the standard atmosphere for?
notes.back: It is a set of standard conditions used as a reference point, so aircraft performance results can be compared.
notes.explanation: Atmospheric conditions vary continuously and are rarely the same on two days, or even two successive flights.
notes.example: Like par on a golf course: a fixed reference to measure real rounds against.
notes.evidence: The conditions in the atmosphere vary continuously, and it is generally not possible to obtain exactly the same set of conditions on two different days or even on two successive flights. For this reason, a set group of standards must be used as a point of reference.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Standard Atmosphere”, p. 5-36

notes.front: What is density altitude?
notes.back: The altitude whose standard air density matches the density actually present.
notes.explanation: It is not necessarily the true altitude.
notes.example: Like judging a hot airfield by the thinner air it behaves as if it had.
notes.evidence: A density altitude of 15,000 ft is the altitude at which the density is the same as that considered standard for 15,000 ft. Remember, however, that density altitude is not necessarily true altitude.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Atmospheric Density”, p. 5-34

notes.front: What is an aerofoil (“airfoil” in FAA usage)?
notes.back: Any device that creates a force, by Bernoulli’s principle or Newton’s laws, when air flows over its surface.
notes.explanation: Wings, propeller blades, helicopter rotor blades and turbofan fan blades are all aerofoils.
notes.example: Like a hand held flat out of a car window that rises when tilted.
notes.evidence: An airfoil is any device that creates a force, based on Bernoulli’s principles or Newton’s laws, when air is caused to flow over the surface of the device. An airfoil can be the wing of an airplane, the blade of a propeller, the rotor blade of a helicopter, or the fan blade of a turbofan engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Airfoils”, p. 5-38

notes.front: What is the camber of a wing?
notes.back: The curvature of its top and bottom surfaces.
notes.explanation: The top camber is usually much more pronounced, except on a symmetrical aerofoil, which is the same top and bottom.
notes.example: Like the arch of a bird’s wing seen end-on.
notes.evidence: The camber of a wing is the curvature which is present on top and bottom surfaces. The camber on the top is much more pronounced, unless the wing is a symmetrical airfoil, which has the same camber top and bottom.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Camber”, p. 5-38

notes.front: What is the chord line of a wing?
notes.back: An imaginary straight line from the wing’s leading edge to its trailing edge.
notes.explanation: Wing angles are measured from it, including the one it makes with the aeroplane’s longitudinal axis.
notes.example: Like a ruler laid from front to back across a wing’s cross-section.
notes.evidence: The chord line is an imaginary straight line running from the wing’s leading edge to its trailing edge. The angle between the chord line and the longitudinal axis of the airplane is known as the angle of incidence.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Chord Line”, p. 5-38

notes.front: What is the relative wind in normal flight?
notes.back: Airflow in the opposite direction to the aircraft’s flightpath.
notes.explanation: It relates the direction of the airflow to the aircraft wing.
notes.example: Like the breeze a cyclist feels on a completely still day.
notes.evidence: The relative wind is a relationship between the direction of airflow and the aircraft wing. In normal flight circumstances, the relative wind is the opposite direction of the aircraft flightpath.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Relative Wind”, p. 5-38

notes.front: What is the angle of attack (AOA)?
notes.back: The angle between the chord line and the relative wind.
notes.explanation: Lift increases as it increases, until too great an angle lets the airflow separate from the wing.
notes.example: Like tilting a hand further up into the airflow from a car window.
notes.evidence: The angle between the chord line and the relative wind is the angle of attack. As the angle of attack increases, the lift on the wing increases. If the angle of attack becomes too great, the airflow can separate from the wing and the lift
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Angle of Attack”, p. 5-38

notes.front: What is the angle of incidence of a wing?
notes.back: The angle between the wing chord line and the horizontal plane through the aircraft’s longitudinal axis.
notes.explanation: It is a design feature: many aeroplanes are designed with more of it at the wing root than at the tip.
notes.example: Like the tilt built into a shelf bracket, fixed when it is made rather than chosen later.
notes.evidence: The angle of incidence of a wing is the angle formed by the intersection of the wing chord line and the horizontal plane passing through the longitudinal axis of the aircraft. Many airplanes are designed with a greater angle of incidence at the root of the wing than at the tip
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Airfoils”, p. 5-39

notes.front: What is the boundary layer?
notes.back: A very thin layer of air lying over the surface of the wing and all other surfaces of the aeroplane.
notes.explanation: Because air has viscosity, the layer tends to adhere to the surface.
notes.example: Like the film of honey that clings to a spoon.
notes.evidence: The boundary layer is a very thin layer of air lying over the surface of the wing and, for that matter, all other surfaces of the airplane. Because air has viscosity, this layer of air tends to adhere to the wing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Boundary Layer Airflow”, p. 5-39

notes.front: What causes wingtip vortices?
notes.back: Higher-pressure air beneath the wing flowing over the tip toward the top, leaving a trailing spiral whenever lift is produced.
notes.explanation: The vortex is also called wake turbulence.
notes.example: Like the swirl left behind a paddle pulled through water.
notes.evidence: Wingtip vortices are caused by the air beneath the wing, which is at the higher pressure, flowing over the wingtip and up toward the top of the wing. The end result is a spiral or vortex that trails behind the wingtip anytime lift is being produced. This vortex is also referred to as wake turbulence
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Wingtip Vortices”, p. 5-40

notes.front: What is longitudinal stability?
notes.back: The tendency, after pitching up or down about the lateral axis, to return to a properly trimmed angle of attack.
notes.explanation: The lateral axis it involves runs from wingtip to wingtip.
notes.example: Like a dart that straightens itself nose-first after a wobble.
notes.evidence: Longitudinal stability for an airplane involves the tendency for the nose to pitch up or pitch down, rotating around the lateral axis, which is measured from wingtip to wingtip. If an airplane is longitudinally stable, it will return to a properly trimmed angle of attack after the force that upset its flightpath is removed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Longitudinal Stability”, p. 5-41

notes.front: What is lateral stability?
notes.back: Stability around the longitudinal axis: the tendency to bring a low wing back to level.
notes.explanation: The longitudinal axis runs from the aeroplane’s nose to its tail.
notes.example: Like a rocking chair settling back upright.
notes.evidence: Lateral stability of an airplane takes place around the longitudinal axis, which is from the airplane’s nose to its tail. If one wing is lower than the other, good lateral stability will tend to bring the wings back to a level flight attitude.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Lateral Stability”, p. 5-42

notes.front: What is directional stability?
notes.back: Stability around the vertical axis: not being adversely affected by a force that creates yaw.
notes.explanation: The vertical fin provides it, making the aeroplane align with the relative wind.
notes.example: Like the flights on a dart keeping it pointed along its path.
notes.evidence: Movement of the airplane around its vertical axis, and the airplane’s ability to not be adversely affected by a force creating a yaw type of motion, is called directional stability. The vertical fin gives the airplane this stability, causing the airplane to align with the relative wind.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Directional Stability”, p. 5-42

notes.front: What is a Dutch roll?
notes.back: A small oscillation around both the longitudinal and vertical axes.
notes.explanation: It is not considered dangerous but is uncomfortable; airliners typically have yaw dampers that sense and cancel it.
notes.example: Like a boat that wallows side to side while its bow swings left and right.
notes.evidence: A Dutch roll is a small amount of oscillation around both the longitudinal and vertical axes. Although this condition is not considered dangerous, it can produce an uncomfortable feeling for passengers. Commercial airliners typically have yaw dampers that sense a Dutch roll condition and cancel it out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Dutch Roll”, p. 5-42

notes.front: What is a trim tab?
notes.back: A small movable surface on a flight control’s trailing edge that holds the control in a deflected position.
notes.explanation: Trim tabs can be controlled from the flight deck.
notes.example: Like a door wedge that keeps a door open with nobody holding it.
notes.evidence: Trim tabs are small movable surfaces that attach to the trailing edge of flight controls. These tabs can be controlled from the flight deck, and their purpose is to create an aerodynamic force that keeps the flight control in a deflected position.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Tabs, Trim Tabs”, p. 5-44

notes.front: What are vortex generators?
notes.back: Short aerofoils, in pairs on a wing’s upper surface, that pull high-energy air down into the boundary layer.
notes.explanation: By doing so they prevent airflow separation.
notes.example: Like small stirring paddles that mix fresh air into a sluggish layer.
notes.evidence: Vortex generators are short airfoils, arranged in pairs, located on the wing’s upper surface. They are positioned such that they pull high-energy air down into the boundary layer region and prevent airflow separation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Boundary Layer Control”, p. 5-40

notes.front: What is a shock wave, in the handbook’s terms?
notes.back: Sound energy piling up on an aeroplane flying at the speed of sound.
notes.explanation: The piling-up begins on top of the wing and eventually attaches to the leading and trailing edges.
notes.example: Like the bow wave heaped up in front of a fast boat.
notes.evidence: At this point the sound energy starts to pile up, initially on the top of the wing, and eventually attaching itself to the wing leading and trailing edges. This piling up of sound energy is called a shock wave.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Shock Waves”, p. 5-47

notes.front: In high-speed flight, what is aerodynamic heating?
notes.back: Heat that builds up on an aeroplane’s surface because of air friction.
notes.explanation: The handbook counts it among the problems of high-speed flight.
notes.example: Like a hand warming as it is rubbed quickly along a rope.
notes.evidence: One of the problems with airplanes and high-speed flight is the heat that builds up on the airplane’s surface because of air friction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Aerodynamic Heating”, p. 5-49

notes.front: What is the only way to change the mass of an object?
notes.back: Add or take away atoms.
notes.explanation: Mass does not change with the object’s place in the universe or with a change of state.
notes.evidence: The mass of an object does not change regardless of where you take it in the universe, or with a change of state. The only way to change the mass of an object is to add or take away atoms.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Mass & Weight”, p. 5-1

notes.front: A part weighs 64.4 lb on earth. What is its mass?
notes.back: B: 2 slugs
notes.choices:
A) 64.4 slugs
B) 2 slugs
C) 0.5 slug
D) 2,074 slugs
notes.choicesExplained: A takes weight as mass. C inverts the ratio. D multiplies by gravity instead of dividing.
notes.explanation: On earth, 32.2 lb corresponds to a mass of 1 slug, so 64.4 lb is 2 slugs.
notes.evidence: The acceleration due to gravity here on earth is 32.2 feet per second per second (32.2 fps/s). An object weighing 32.2 pounds (lb) here on earth is said to have a mass of 1 slug.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Mass & Weight”, p. 5-1

notes.front: A tank holds 10 ft³ of a liquid that weighs 624 lb. What is the liquid’s density?
notes.back: B: 62.4 lb/ft³
notes.choices:
A) 6.24 lb/ft³
B) 62.4 lb/ft³
C) 634 lb/ft³
D) 6,240 lb/ft³
notes.choicesExplained: A divides by 100, not 10. C adds instead of dividing. D multiplies instead of dividing.
notes.explanation: Density is weight divided by volume: 624 ÷ 10 = 62.4 lb/ft³.
notes.evidence: To find the density of a substance, its weight and volume must be known. Its weight is then divided by its volume to find the weight per unit volume.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Density”, p. 5-2

notes.front: A fuel has a specific gravity of 0.75. What does 1 ft³ of it weigh, taking water as 62.4 lb/ft³?
notes.choicesExplained: C forgets to multiply by water’s weight. B divides by the specific gravity. D is water itself.
notes.explanation: Multiply water’s weight per cubic foot by the specific gravity: 62.4 × 0.75 = 46.8 lb.
notes.evidence: For example, if a certain hydraulic fluid has a specific gravity of 0.8, 1 ft3 of the liquid weighs 0.8 times as much as 1 ft3 of water: 62.4 times 0.8, or 49.92 lb.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Specific Gravity”, p. 5-2

notes.front: A fully charged storage battery sits on a shelf. Which group of potential energy does it hold?
notes.back: A: Energy that produces work through chemical action
notes.choices:
A) Energy that produces work through chemical action
B) Energy due to distortion of an elastic body
C) None: a battery holds kinetic energy
D) Energy due to position
notes.choicesExplained: D is the group for raised objects, such as an aeroplane on jacks. B is the group for a stretched bungee cord or compressed spring. C is wrong: nothing is moving, so the energy is stored.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists storage batteries, with aviation gasoline and food, in the third group.
notes.evidence: Examples of the first group are water in an elevated reservoir or an airplane raised off the ground with jacks; a stretched bungee cord on a Piper TriPacer or compressed spring are examples of the second group; and energy in aviation gasoline, food, or storage batteries are examples of the third group.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Potential Energy”, p. 5-3

notes.front: A tug’s speed doubles while its mass stays the same. What happens to its kinetic energy?
notes.back: B: It becomes four times as great
notes.choices:
A) It doubles
B) It becomes four times as great
C) It stays the same
D) It halves
notes.choicesExplained: A treats velocity as if it were not squared. C and D ignore that kinetic energy grows with velocity.
notes.explanation: Velocity is squared in the formula, so doubling it multiplies kinetic energy by four.
notes.evidence: To calculate the kinetic energy for something in motion, the following formula is used: Kinetic Energy = 1⁄2 Mass × Velocity2
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Kinetic Energy”, p. 5-3

notes.front: One BTU of heat energy = {{c1::778}} ft-lb of work.
notes.explanation: Many experiments established this relationship between heat and mechanical energy.
notes.evidence: A definite relationship exists between heat and mechanical energy. This relationship has been established and verified by many experiments which show that: One BTU of heat energy = 778 ft-lb of work
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Heat Energy Units”, p. 5-19

notes.front: The handbook gives 1 lb of aviation gasoline as 18,900 BTU. How much work could half a pound do?
notes.choicesExplained: B stops at BTU and never converts to work. C is a whole pound. D divides a whole pound's 18,900 BTU by 778 instead of multiplying.
notes.explanation: 9,450 BTU × 778 ft-lb per BTU = 7,352,100 ft-lb, half the 14,704,200 ft-lb in a full pound.
notes.evidence: One pound of aviation gas contains 18,900 BTU of heat energy, and each BTU is capable of 778 ft-lb of work. So, when we multiply 778 by 18,900, we find that one pound of aviation gas is capable of 14,704,200 ft-lb of work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Potential Energy”, p. 5-3

notes.front: Two mechanics push hard on a parked aeroplane with its brakes set, and it does not move. How much work have they done, in the mechanical sense?
notes.back: A: None
notes.choices:
A) None
B) Their force multiplied by the aeroplane’s weight
C) Their force multiplied by the time spent pushing
D) Half the aeroplane’s weight, in foot-pounds
notes.choicesExplained: C brings in time, which belongs to power, not work. B multiplies two forces. D has no basis in the definition.
notes.explanation: Work needs an object displaced some distance against a resistive force; nothing moved, so none was done.
notes.evidence: According to the technical definition, no work had been done when the men were pushing against the aircraft. By definition, work is accomplished only when an object is displaced some distance against a resistive force.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Work”, p. 5-4

notes.front: What is static friction, and how does it change once an object moves?
notes.back: The resistance of being set in motion; once moving, it is greatly reduced.
notes.explanation: So a smaller force keeps something moving than was needed to start it.
notes.evidence: static friction, which is the resistance of being set in motion, would be greater than the force exerted by the engine. However, once the cars are in motion, the static friction is greatly reduced and a smaller force is required to keep the train in motion than was required to start it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Static Friction”, p. 5-5

notes.front: A 40,000-lb aeroplane is being towed on concrete, where μ for its tyres is about 0.02. Roughly what towing force keeps it rolling once it is moving?
notes.back: B: 800 lb
notes.choicesExplained: A uses the full weight as the resistance. D and C slip the decimal point.
notes.explanation: Rolling friction uses the sliding-friction equation with a much smaller μ: 0.02 × 40,000 lb = 800 lb.
notes.evidence: This force may be computed by the same equation used in computing sliding friction, but the values of “m” will be much smaller. For example, the value of “m” for rubber tires on concrete or macadam is about 0.02.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Rolling Friction”, p. 5-6

notes.front: A winch raises a 3,300-lb load 10 ft in 1 minute. What horsepower does this represent?
notes.back: C: 1 hp
notes.choices:
A) 10 hp
B) 0.1 hp
C) 1 hp
D) 60 hp
notes.choicesExplained: B and A slip a factor of 10. D treats the 1 minute as 1 second: 33,000 ft-lb per second ÷ 550 = 60.
notes.explanation: Power is 3,300 lb × 10 ft ÷ 1 min = 33,000 ft-lb/min, and dividing by 33,000 gives 1 hp.
notes.evidence: 1 hp = 33,000 ft-lb/min. 1 hp = 375 mile pounds per hour (mi-lb/hr.) 1 hp = 746 watts (electricity conversion) To convert power to horsepower, divide the power by the appropriate conversion based on the units being used.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Power”, p. 5-6

notes.front: Torque = force × {{c1::distance}}, where the distance is the one along which the force is applied.
notes.explanation: Unlike in the work formula, it is not a distance the object moves; with torque, nothing has to move.
notes.evidence: Torque = Force × distance Even though this formula looks the same as the other formula for calculating work, recognize that the distance value in this formula is not the linear distance an object moves, but rather the distance along which the force is applied. Notice that with torque nothing had to move
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Torque”, p. 5-7

notes.front: An engine produces 200 hp at 2,626 rpm. How much torque is it producing?
notes.back: C: 400 lb-ft
notes.choices:
A) 200 lb-ft
B) 1,050,400 lb-ft
C) 400 lb-ft
D) 40 lb-ft
notes.choicesExplained: A halves the result. B forgets to divide by rpm. D slips the decimal point.
notes.explanation: Torque = horsepower × 5,252 ÷ rpm = 200 × 5,252 ÷ 2,626 = 400 lb-ft.
notes.evidence: Torque = Horsepower × 5,252 ÷ rpm
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Torque”, p. 5-7

notes.front: What are the six simple machines named in the handbook?
notes.back: The lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, screw and gear.
notes.explanation: Physicists recognise only two basic principles among them: the lever and the inclined plane.
notes.evidence: There are only six simple machines. They are the lever, the pulley, the wheel and axle, the inclined plane, the screw, and the gear. Physicists, however, recognize only two basic principles in machines: the lever and the inclined plane.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Simple Machines”, p. 5-7

notes.front: Which of these machines operates on the principle of the lever?
notes.back: C: A pair of meshed gears
notes.choices:
A) A wedge
B) A screw
C) A pair of meshed gears
D) A loading ramp
notes.choicesExplained: A and B use the principle of the inclined plane. D is itself an inclined plane.
notes.explanation: Pulleys, the wheel and axle, and gears work on the lever principle; the wedge and screw on the inclined plane.
notes.evidence: The pulley (block and tackle), the wheel and axle, and gears operate on the machine principle of the lever. The wedge and the screw use the principle of the inclined plane.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Simple Machines”, p. 5-7

notes.front: Where is the fulcrum in a first class lever?
notes.back: Between the effort and the resistance.
notes.explanation: A seesaw is a good example of a first class lever.
notes.evidence: In the first class lever, the fulcrum is located between the effort and the resistance. As mentioned earlier, the seesaw is a good example of a lever, and it happens to be a first class lever.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “First Class Lever”, p. 5-8

notes.front: Where are the fulcrum, effort and resistance in a second class lever?
notes.back: Fulcrum at one end, effort at the other, resistance between them.
notes.explanation: A wheelbarrow is a good example: the wheel is the fulcrum, the handles take the effort and the bucket holds the load.
notes.evidence: The second class lever has the fulcrum at one end and the effort is applied at the other end. The resistance is somewhere between these points. A wheelbarrow is a good example of a second class lever
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Second Class Lever”, p. 5-9

notes.front: In a third class lever, where is the effort applied?
notes.back: Between the fulcrum and the resistance.
notes.explanation: A retractable main landing gear is the handbook’s example of this class.
notes.evidence: Third class levers are easily recognized because the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the resistance. The retractable main landing gear on an airplane is a good example of a third class lever.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Third Class Lever”, p. 5-9

notes.front: A first class lever has its load 10 in from the fulcrum and the effort 50 in from it. What effort lifts a 400-lb load, and what is the mechanical advantage?
notes.choicesExplained: D swaps the arms. B ignores the arms altogether. C has the right effort but inverts the mechanical advantage.
notes.explanation: Effort × 50 in = 400 lb × 10 in, so effort = 80 lb; force out ÷ force in = 400 ÷ 80 = 5.
notes.evidence: When calculating how much effort is required to lift a specific weight, or how much weight can be lifted by a specific effort, the following formula can be used. Effort (E) × Effort Arm (L) = Resistance (R) × Resistance Arm (l)
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “First Class Lever”, p. 5-8

notes.front: What determines the mechanical advantage of a block and tackle?
notes.back: The number of ropes supporting the weight.
notes.explanation: The rope where the effort is applied is not counted.
notes.evidence: notice there are four ropes supporting the weight and a fifth rope where the effort is applied. The number of weight supporting ropes determines the mechanical advantage of a block and tackle, so in this case the mechanical advantage is four.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Block and Tackle”, p. 5-10

notes.front: A block and tackle has six ropes supporting the load and a seventh rope where the effort is applied. Ignoring friction, what effort lifts 900 lb?
notes.back: D: 150 lb
notes.choicesExplained: B counts the effort rope as well. C is a single fixed pulley’s result. A multiplies instead of dividing.
notes.explanation: Six weight-supporting ropes give a mechanical advantage of six: 900 ÷ 6 = 150 lb.
notes.evidence: The number of weight supporting ropes determines the mechanical advantage of a block and tackle, so in this case the mechanical advantage is four. If the weight was 200 lb, it would require a 50 lb effort to lift it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Block and Tackle”, p. 5-10

notes.front: When a large gear drives a small one, what happens to the small gear’s speed and force?
notes.back: It turns faster and has less available force.
notes.explanation: To gain force instead, the small gear must turn the large one.
notes.evidence: This analysis tells us that when a large gear drives a small one, the small one turns faster and has less available force. In order to be a force gaining machine, the small gear needs to turn the large one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “The Gear”, p. 5-10

notes.front: A 20-tooth pinion drives a 60-tooth gear. Compared with the pinion, how does the larger gear turn?
notes.back: B: At one-third the speed, with more force
notes.choices:
A) Three times faster, with less force
B) At one-third the speed, with more force
C) At the same speed and force
D) Faster and with more force
notes.choicesExplained: A describes a large gear driving a small one. C would need equal teeth. D is impossible: a machine cannot gain force and speed together.
notes.explanation: The small gear turning the large one makes a force-gaining machine, trading speed for force.
notes.evidence: In order to be a force gaining machine, the small gear needs to turn the large one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “The Gear”, p. 5-10

notes.front: What is the mechanical advantage of a worm gear driving a spur gear?
notes.back: Equal to the number of teeth on the spur gear.
notes.explanation: One complete turn of the worm moves the spur gear by only one tooth.
notes.evidence: One complete revolution of the worm gear only makes the spur gear move an amount equal to one tooth. The mechanical advantage is equal to the number of teeth on the spur gear
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “The Gear”, p. 5-10

notes.front: On an inclined plane, what are the effort arm and the resistance arm?
notes.back: The effort arm is the length of the incline; the resistance arm is its vertical height.
notes.explanation: An incline five times longer than its height gives a mechanical advantage of five.
notes.evidence: With an inclined plane, the length of the incline is the effort arm and the vertical height of the incline is the resistance arm. If the length of the incline is five times greater than the height, there will be a force advantage, or mechanical advantage, of five.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Inclined Plane”, p. 5-11

notes.front: A mechanic sketches a ramp 30 in long that rises 5 in, to push one 1,200-lb wheel load onto a scale. Ignoring friction, what are the mechanical advantage and the push needed?
notes.choicesExplained: A inverts the arms, taking 5 ÷ 30 as the mechanical advantage. D has the right mechanical advantage but multiplies the load by it instead of dividing. B uses the rise as if it were the mechanical advantage.
notes.explanation: Length ÷ height = 30 ÷ 5 = 6, so the push is 1,200 lb ÷ 6 = 200 lb.
notes.evidence: With an inclined plane, the length of the incline is the effort arm and the vertical height of the incline is the resistance arm. If the length of the incline is five times greater than the height, there will be a force advantage, or mechanical advantage, of five.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Inclined Plane”, p. 5-11

notes.front: Which of the five forms of stress tries to pull an object apart?
notes.back: Tension.
notes.explanation: The five forms are tension, compression, torsion, bending and shear.
notes.evidence: The five forms are tension, compression, torsion, bending, and shear. Tension Tension is a force that tries to pull an object apart.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Tension”, p. 5-12

notes.front: Which stress tries to crush an object, as when a rivet is driven?
notes.back: Compression.
notes.explanation: Assembling a sheet metal aeroplane with rivets is the handbook’s example.
notes.evidence: Compression is a force that tries to crush an object. An excellent example of compression is when a sheet metal airplane is assembled using the fastener known as a rivet.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Compression”, p. 5-13

notes.front: Which stress does a shaft carry when torque twists it, and what two stresses make it up?
notes.back: Torsion, made up of tension and compression.
notes.explanation: Tension acts at a diagonal to the shaft and compression at 90 degrees to the tension.
notes.evidence: Torsion is the stress an object experiences when it is twisted, which is what happens when torque is applied to a shaft. Torsion is made up of two other stresses: tension and compression. When a shaft is twisted, tension is experienced at a diagonal to the shaft and compression acts 90 degrees to the tension.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Torsion”, p. 5-13

notes.front: Which stress acts on a clevis bolt securing a cable fitting to the airframe?
notes.back: Shear.
notes.explanation: A shear force tries to cut or slice through, like a knife through butter.
notes.evidence: When a shear stress is applied to an object, the force tries to cut or slice through, like a knife cutting through butter. A clevis bolt, which is often used to secure a cable to a part of the airframe, has shear stress acting on it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Shear”, p. 5-13

notes.front: An aeroplane is parked on its landing gear. Under bending, which part of the wing is in compression?
notes.back: A: The bottom skin
notes.choices:
A) The bottom skin
B) Neither: a parked wing has no bending stress
C) Both skins equally
D) The top skin
notes.choicesExplained: D is the case in flight, when lift bends the wing up. B and C ignore gravity bending the wing down.
notes.explanation: On the ground, gravity bends the wing downward, putting the bottom in compression and the top in tension.
notes.evidence: When the airplane is on the ground sitting on its landing gear, the force of gravity tries to bend the wing downward, subjecting the bottom of the wing to compression and the top of the wing tension.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Bending”, p. 5-13

notes.front: On a turbine engine test cell, the thrust reading rises. What did the strain gauges physically sense?
notes.back: B: More distortion from the engine pulling against them
notes.choices:
A) A higher exhaust temperature
B) More distortion from the engine pulling against them
C) A higher rotor speed
D) A greater fuel flow
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are not what a strain gauge measures; it responds to distortion under force.
notes.explanation: The engine’s thrust pulls against the gauges, and the amount of distortion is translated into thrust.
notes.evidence: On turbine engine test cells, the thrust of the engine is typically measured by what are called strain gages. When the force, or thrust, of the engine is pulling out against the strain gages, the amount of distortion is measured and then translated into the appropriate thrust reading.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Strain”, p. 5-14

notes.front: A tug drives round a circular apron at a steady 10 mph. Which is true?
notes.back: B: Its speed is constant but its velocity keeps changing
notes.choices:
A) Its speed and velocity are both constant
B) Its speed is constant but its velocity keeps changing
C) Its speed keeps changing but its velocity is constant
D) Neither its speed nor its velocity changes
notes.choicesExplained: A and D forget that velocity includes direction. C reverses the two quantities.
notes.explanation: Going round a circle means constantly changing direction, and velocity includes direction.
notes.evidence: The airplane is constantly changing direction because of the circular pattern, which means the airplane is constantly changing velocity. The reason for this is the fact that velocity includes direction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Speed and Velocity”, p. 5-15

notes.front: A tug speeds up from 5 mph to 20 mph in 5 seconds. What is its average acceleration?
notes.back: D: 3 mph per second
notes.choices:
A) 4 mph per second
B) 15 mph per second
C) 25 mph per second
D) 3 mph per second
notes.choicesExplained: A divides the final speed alone by time. B forgets to divide by time. C adds the speeds.
notes.explanation: Acceleration = (final velocity − initial velocity) ÷ time = (20 − 5) ÷ 5 = 3 mph per second.
notes.evidence: To calculate acceleration, the following formula is used. Acceleration (A) = Velocity Final (Vf) − Velocity Initial (Vi) Time (t)
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Acceleration”, p. 5-16

notes.front: A tow tractor stops suddenly and an unsecured toolbox slides forward off its bed. Which principle best explains this?
notes.back: A: Newton’s first law (inertia)
notes.choices:
A) Newton’s first law (inertia)
B) Bernoulli’s principle
C) Pascal’s law
D) Newton’s third law
notes.choicesExplained: D concerns action and reaction pairs. B concerns fluid velocity and pressure. C concerns pressure in a confined fluid.
notes.explanation: The box keeps moving at the same speed and direction until an external force acts: that is inertia.
notes.evidence: Inertia is responsible for the discomfort felt when an airplane is brought to a sudden halt in the parking area and the passengers are thrown forward in their seats.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Newton’s Law of Motion, First Law”, p. 5-16

notes.front: An engine moves 100 lb of air per second, accelerating it from 0 to 966 fps. Using force = weight × (final − initial velocity) ÷ (gravity × time), how much thrust does it make?
notes.choicesExplained: B forgets to divide by gravity. C and D slip the decimal point.
notes.explanation: Dividing by gravity turns the air’s weight into mass: 100 × 966 ÷ 32.2 = 3,000 lb.
notes.evidence: Earlier in this chapter, it was determined that mass equals weight divided by gravity, and acceleration equals velocity final minus velocity initial divided by time.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Newton’s Law of Motion, Second Law”, p. 5-16

notes.front: A propeller pushes a stream of air backwards with a force of 800 lb. What does the air do to the propeller blades?
notes.back: D: Pushes them forward with 800 lb
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because air is a fluid
B) Pushes them forward with 400 lb
C) Pushes them backward with 800 lb
D) Pushes them forward with 800 lb
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that forces always come in pairs. C gives the right size but the wrong direction. B halves the reaction.
notes.explanation: By the third law the reaction equals the action and is opposite, and that forward force moves the aircraft.
notes.evidence: When an aircraft propeller pushes a stream of air backward with a force of 500 lb, the air pushes the blades forward with a force of 500 lb. This forward force causes the aircraft to move forward.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Newton’s Law of Motion, Third Law”, p. 5-17

notes.front: In circular motion, what is centrifugal force?
notes.back: The force equal to the centripetal force but acting in the opposite direction.
notes.explanation: The string pulls the object inward, and the object pulls back on the string, obeying Newton’s third law.
notes.evidence: The string exerts a centripetal force on the object, and the object exerts an equal but opposite force on the string, obeying Newton’s third law of motion. The force that is equal to centripetal force, but acting in an opposite direction, is called centrifugal force.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Circular Motion”, p. 5-17

notes.front: An engine produces 150 hp while burning fuel with the potential to make 600 hp. What is its thermal efficiency?
notes.back: B: 25 percent
notes.choices:
A) 400 percent
B) 25 percent
C) 75 percent
D) 450 percent
notes.choicesExplained: A inverts the ratio. C is the share wasted, not used. D subtracts instead of dividing.
notes.explanation: Thermal efficiency = horsepower produced ÷ potential horsepower in fuel = 150 ÷ 600 = 25 percent.
notes.evidence: The formula for calculating thermal efficiency is: Thermal Efficiency = Horsepower Produced ÷ Potential Horsepower in Fuel
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Heat Energy and Thermal Efficiency”, p. 5-19

notes.front: What does heat transfer by conduction require?
notes.back: Physical contact between an object with more heat energy and one with less.
notes.explanation: Heat always migrates from areas of high heat energy to areas of low heat energy.
notes.evidence: Heat transfer always takes place by areas of high heat energy migrating to areas of low heat energy. Heat transfer by conduction requires that there be physical contact between an object that has a large amount of heat energy and one that has a smaller amount of heat energy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Conduction”, p. 5-19

notes.front: What is convection?
notes.back: Heat transfer by movement of a heated fluid, gas or liquid.
notes.explanation: Air heated round a hot light bulb moves upward and carries the heat away.
notes.evidence: Convection is the process by which heat is transferred by movement of a heated fluid (gas or liquid). For example, an incandescent light bulb will, when heated, become increasingly hotter until the air surrounding it begins to move. The motion of the air is upward.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Convection”, p. 5-20

notes.front: Sunlight through a hangar’s skylight warms a painted panel below, though the glass itself stays fairly cool. Which method of heat transfer is at work?
notes.back: B: Radiation
notes.choices:
A) Conduction
B) Radiation
C) Conduction through the glass, then convection
D) Convection
notes.choicesExplained: A and C need contact, and the glass is not what heats the panel. D needs a moving heated fluid.
notes.explanation: Radiant heat can pass through a medium without heating it, as through greenhouse glass.
notes.evidence: Second, radiant heat may pass through a medium without heating it. In application, the air inside a greenhouse may be much warmer than the glass through which the sun’s rays pass.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Radiation”, p. 5-21

notes.front: Degrees Fahrenheit = ({{c1::1.8}} × degrees Celsius) + 32.
notes.explanation: The reverse is degrees Celsius = (degrees Fahrenheit − 32) × 5/9.
notes.evidence: Degrees Fahrenheit = (1.8 × Degrees Celsius) + 32 Degrees Celsius = (Degrees Fahrenheit – 32) × 5⁄9
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Temperature”, p. 5-21

notes.front: How are Kelvin and Rankine temperatures found from Celsius and Fahrenheit?
notes.back: Kelvin = °C + 273; Rankine = °F + 460.
notes.explanation: Rankine is commonly used to turn Fahrenheit readings into absolute values for calculations.
notes.evidence: Degrees Kelvin = Degrees Celsius + 273 Degrees Rankine = Degrees Fahrenheit + 460 For purposes of calculations, the Rankine scale is commonly used to convert Fahrenheit to absolute.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Temperature”, p. 5-21

notes.front: A maintenance manual gives a temperature limit of 40 °C. What is that in °F?
notes.choicesExplained: B forgets to multiply by 1.8. C applies the Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula the wrong way round. D converts to Kelvin instead.
notes.evidence: Degrees Fahrenheit = (1.8 × Degrees Celsius) + 32
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Temperature”, p. 5-21

notes.front: Which temperature scales are used more in scientific work, and which is common in the United States?
notes.back: Kelvin and Centigrade in scientific work; Fahrenheit in the United States.
notes.explanation: So some technical manuals give directions and operating instructions in Kelvin or Centigrade.
notes.evidence: The Kelvin and Centigrade scales are used more extensively in scientific work; therefore, some technical manuals may use these scales in giving directions and operating instructions. The Fahrenheit scale is commonly used in the United States
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Temperature”, p. 5-22

notes.front: Expansion = coefficient of expansion × length × {{c1::rise in temperature}}.
notes.explanation: All three must be known to estimate how much an object expands.
notes.evidence: To estimate the expansion of any object, such as a steel rail, it is necessary to know three things about it: its length, the rise in temperature to which it is subjected, and its coefficient of expansion. This relationship is expressed by the equation: Expansion = (coefficient) × (length) × (rise in temperature)
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Thermal Expansion/Contraction”, p. 5-22

notes.front: An aluminium tube 10 ft long, with a coefficient of expansion of 25 × 10⁻⁶ per °C, warms by 40 °C. How much longer does it get?
notes.choices:
A) 0.1 ft
B) 0.01 ft
C) 0.001 ft
D) 1 ft
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D slip the decimal point.
notes.evidence: This relationship is expressed by the equation: Expansion = (coefficient) × (length) × (rise in temperature)
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Thermal Expansion/Contraction”, p. 5-22

notes.front: Why must thermal expansion be considered when designing airframes and powerplants?
notes.back: A part placed where it cannot expand freely exerts a tremendous force.
notes.explanation: Even a very small change in length matters when the part is restrained.
notes.evidence: if the rod were placed where it could not expand freely, there would be a tremendous force exerted due to thermal expansion. Thus, thermal expansion must be taken into consideration when designing airframes, power plants, or related equipment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Thermal Expansion/Contraction”, p. 5-22

notes.front: Standard day atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psi. What is it in inches of mercury, millimetres of mercury and millibars?
notes.back: 29.92 inches, 760 millimetres and 1013.2 millibars.
notes.explanation: One psi equals 2.04 inches of mercury, 51.7 mm of mercury or 68.9 millibars.
notes.evidence: Standard day atmospheric pressure is equal to 14.7 psi, 29.92 inches of mercury ("Hg), 760 millimeters of mercury (mm hg), or 1013.2 millibars. The relationship between these units of measure is as follows: 1 psi = 2.04 "Hg 1 psi = 51.7 mm Hg 1 psi = 68.9 millibars
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Pressure”, p. 5-22

notes.front: A 240-lb load rests evenly on a pad with a surface area of 12 in². What is the average pressure under it?
notes.back: B: 20 psi
notes.choices:
A) 2,880 psi
B) 20 psi
C) 252 psi
D) 0.05 psi
notes.choicesExplained: A multiplies instead of dividing. C adds. D divides area by force.
notes.explanation: Pressure is force per unit area: 240 lb ÷ 12 in² = 20 psi.
notes.evidence: If a 100-lb weight was placed on top of a block with a surface area of 10 in2, the average weight distribution would be 10 lb for each of the square inches (100 ÷ 10), or 10 psi.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Pressure”, p. 5-22

notes.front: Absolute pressure (psia) = gauge pressure + {{c1::atmospheric pressure}}.
notes.explanation: A psia instrument on a stopped engine’s oil system would still read atmospheric pressure.
notes.evidence: Absolute pressure is equal to gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure. If someone hooked up a psia indicating instrument to an engine’s oil system, the gauge would read atmospheric pressure when the engine was not running.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Absolute Pressure”, p. 5-23

notes.front: A piston engine’s manifold pressure may be below atmospheric when not supercharged and above it when supercharged. Which kind of gauge shows this?
notes.back: C: An absolute-pressure (psia) instrument
notes.choices:
A) A gauge-pressure (psig) instrument
B) A differential-pressure (psid) instrument
C) An absolute-pressure (psia) instrument
D) A vacuum gauge reading below atmospheric only
notes.choicesExplained: A reads only above ambient. B compares two points in a system. D cannot show readings above atmospheric.
notes.explanation: Only the absolute pressure gauge has the flexibility to show readings both below and above atmospheric.
notes.evidence: than atmospheric if it is supercharged. The only gauge that has the flexibility to show this variety of readings is the absolute pressure gauge.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Absolute Pressure”, p. 5-23

notes.front: The oil filter differential pressure light comes on in a turbine engine’s flight deck. What does it most likely indicate?
notes.back: D: The filter is starting to clog
notes.choices:
A) The oil has become too cold to measure
B) The oil pump has stopped
C) Atmospheric pressure has fallen
D) The filter is starting to clog
notes.choicesExplained: B would drop both readings, not widen the gap between them. C affects both sides of the filter alike. A is not what a differential across the filter measures.
notes.explanation: A clogging filter increases the pressure drop across it, which eventually switches on the advisory light.
notes.evidence: Across anything that poses a resistance to flow, like an oil filter, there will be a drop in pressure. If the filter starts to clog, the pressure drop will become greater, eventually causing the advisory light on the flight deck to come on.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Differential Pressure”, p. 5-23

notes.front: A system gauge reads 50 psig on a standard day at sea level. What is the absolute pressure?
notes.back: D: 64.7 psia
notes.choices:
A) 35.3 psia
B) 79.92 psia
C) 50 psia
D) 64.7 psia
notes.choicesExplained: A subtracts atmospheric pressure. C forgets it. B adds inches of mercury to psi.
notes.explanation: Absolute = gauge + atmospheric = 50 + 14.7 = 64.7 psia.
notes.evidence: Absolute pressure is equal to gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Absolute Pressure”, p. 5-23

notes.front: 20 ft³ of nitrogen at 300 psia is compressed to 10 ft³ at constant temperature. What is its new pressure?
notes.back: C: 600 psia
notes.choices:
A) 150 psia
B) 300 psia
C) 600 psia
D) 3,000 psia
notes.choicesExplained: A treats pressure as rising with volume. B ignores the change. D slips a factor of 10.
notes.explanation: At constant temperature, halving the volume doubles the absolute pressure: 20 × 300 = 10 × P₂, so P₂ = 600 psia.
notes.evidence: The following formula is used for Boyle’s law calculations. Remember, pressure needs to be in the absolute. Volume 1 × Pressure 1 = Volume 2 × Pressure 2
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Boyle’s Law”, p. 5-24

notes.front: A sealed gas cylinder at 60 °F reads 505.3 psig. Its volume cannot change, and it warms to 120 °F. What will the gauge read?
notes.back: B: 565.3 psig
notes.choices:
A) 1,010.6 psig
B) 565.3 psig
C) 451.5 psig
D) 580 psig
notes.choicesExplained: A doubles pressure with Fahrenheit temperature. D forgets to convert back to gauge pressure. C has the temperature ratio upside down.
notes.explanation: In absolute terms, 520 psia × 580 °R ÷ 520 °R = 580 psia, which is 565.3 psig.
notes.evidence: P1T2 = P2T1 For this second formula, pressure and temperature must be in the absolute.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Charles’ Law”, p. 5-25

notes.front: The general gas law, P₁V₁T₂ = P₂V₂T₁, combines Boyle’s law and {{c1::Charles’ law}}.
notes.explanation: One expression then states everything both laws contain.
notes.evidence: By combining Boyle’s and Charles’ laws, a single expression can be derived which states all the information contained in both.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “General Gas Law”, p. 5-25

notes.front: 10 ft³ of gas at 100 psia and 500 °R is compressed to 5 ft³ and warms to 600 °R. What is its new pressure?
notes.back: A: 240 psia
notes.choices:
A) 240 psia
B) 200 psia
C) 166.7 psia
D) 120 psia
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the temperature rise. C applies the temperature ratio upside down. D ignores the volume change.
notes.explanation: Rearranging the general gas law with absolute values: P₂ = 100 × 10 × 600 ÷ (5 × 500) = 240 psia.
