notes.evidence: When using the general gas law formula, temperature and pressure must be in the absolute.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “General Gas Law”, p. 5-25

notes.front: A sealed 2 ft³ float weighing 100 lb is placed in fresh water at 62.4 lb/ft³. What happens?
notes.back: B: It floats
notes.choices:
A) It sinks, weighing 24.8 lb when submerged
B) It floats
C) It sinks, weighing 100 lb when submerged
D) It sinks to the bottom and weighs 124.8 lb
notes.choicesExplained: A and C treat a buoyant force larger than the weight as if it were smaller. D adds the buoyant force to the weight.
notes.explanation: Buoyant force = 2 ft³ × 62.4 lb/ft³ = 124.8 lb, more than the 100 lb weight, so it floats.
notes.evidence: Buoyant Force = Volume of Object × Density of Fluid Displaced If the buoyant force is more than the object weighs, the object will float.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Buoyancy”, p. 5-26

notes.front: What determines the pressure a liquid exerts on the bottom of its container?
notes.back: The height of the liquid, not the shape of the container.
notes.explanation: Containers of different shapes and volumes filled to the same height give the same bottom pressure.
notes.evidence: The pressure exerted on the bottom of a container by a liquid is determined by the height of the liquid and not by the shape of the container.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Fluid Pressure”, p. 5-27

notes.front: What are ram pressure and total pressure?
notes.back: Ram pressure comes from a moving fluid’s velocity; total pressure is ram plus static pressure.
notes.explanation: Static pressure is the part due to the height of a fluid column.
notes.evidence: As identified in the previous paragraph, pressure due to the height of a fluid column is known as static pressure. When a fluid is in motion, and its velocity is converted to pressure, that pressure is known as ram. When ram pressure and static pressure are added together, the result is known as total pressure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Fluid Pressure”, p. 5-27

notes.front: For Pascal’s law problems, force = pressure × {{c1::area}}.
notes.explanation: Rearranged, pressure = force ÷ area and area = force ÷ pressure.
notes.evidence: Force = Pressure × Area In this formula, the force is in units of pounds, the pressure is in pounds per square inch (psi), and the area is in square inches. By transposing the original formula, we have two additional formulas, as follows: Pressure = Force ÷ Area and Area = Force ÷ Pressure
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Pascal’s Law”, p. 5-28

notes.front: A hydraulic system at 1,500 psi acts on an actuator piston of 4 in². What force does the piston produce?
notes.choicesExplained: A divides instead of multiplying. B adds. D slips a factor of 10.
notes.explanation: Force = pressure × area = 1,500 psi × 4 in² = 6,000 lb.
notes.evidence: Force = Pressure × Area In this formula, the force is in units of pounds, the pressure is in pounds per square inch (psi), and the area is in square inches.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Pascal’s Law”, p. 5-28

notes.front: Can a hydraulic system give out more work than is put into it?
notes.back: No; if it gains force, it must lose distance.
notes.explanation: Even the same work out is only reached if the system is 100 percent efficient.
notes.evidence: The same statement holds true for a hydraulic system, that we get no more work out of a hydraulic system than we put in. Since work is equal to force times distance, if we gain force with a hydraulic system, we must lose distance. We only get the same work out, if the system is 100 percent efficient.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Pascal’s Law”, p. 5-28

notes.front: A liquid flows through a venturi. At the narrow throat, compared with the wide ends, how do its velocity and static pressure compare?
notes.back: A: Velocity is higher and pressure lower
notes.choices:
A) Velocity is higher and pressure lower
B) Both are lower
C) Velocity is lower and pressure higher
D) Both are higher
notes.choicesExplained: D and B break Bernoulli’s trade between velocity and pressure. C describes the wide sections, not the throat.
notes.explanation: The same volume must pass through the narrow section, so it moves faster and its static pressure falls.
notes.evidence: As indicated by the velocity gauge reading high and the pressure gauge reading low, in this narrow section, the liquid moves at a higher velocity, producing a lower pressure than that at points A and C.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Bernoulli’s Principle”, p. 5-30

notes.front: How does a float-type carburettor use the venturi principle?
notes.back: Static pressure drops in the venturi, so fuel at higher pressure flows into it and mixes with the air.
notes.explanation: Fuel moves from the carburettor’s higher pressure into the lower-pressure venturi area.
notes.evidence: As the air flows through the carburetor on its way to the engine, it goes through a venturi, where the static pressure is reduced. The fuel in the carburetor, which is under a higher pressure, flows into the lower pressure venturi area and mixes with the air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Bernoulli’s Principle”, p. 5-30

notes.front: What happens to subsonic air flowing through a diverging duct?
notes.back: Its velocity decreases and its static pressure increases.
notes.explanation: The total energy is unchanged: kinetic energy lost as velocity is gained as potential energy in static pressure.
notes.evidence: With the increase in cross-sectional area, the velocity of the air decreases and the static pressure increases. The total energy in the air has not changed. What has been lost in velocity, which is kinetic energy, is gained in static pressure, which is potential energy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Bernoulli’s Principle and Subsonic Flow”, p. 5-37

notes.front: How does Bernoulli’s principle explain the lift on a slow aeroplane’s wing?
notes.back: Air speeds up over the curved top and its static pressure falls; the greater pressure below creates lift.
notes.explanation: The pressure difference between the two surfaces is what creates the lift.
notes.evidence: As the air flow over the top of the wing, the air speeds up, and its static pressure decreases. The static pressure on the bottom of the wing is now greater than the pressure on the top, and this pressure difference creates the lift on the wing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Bernoulli’s Principle”, p. 5-30

notes.front: A wing panel of 5,000 in² has 0.2 psi more static pressure below it than above. How much lift does the difference create?
notes.choicesExplained: A divides area by pressure. C and D slip the decimal point.
notes.explanation: Each square inch gets 0.2 lb of lift: 0.2 × 5,000 = 1,000 lb.
notes.evidence: If the difference in static pressure between the top and bottom is 0.1 psi, there will be 1⁄10 lb of lift for each square inch of surface area.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Bernoulli’s Principle and Subsonic Flow”, p. 5-37

notes.front: How does Newton’s third law explain lift?
notes.back: The wing forces the air downward off its trailing edge; the equal and opposite reacting force is lift.
notes.explanation: A force is needed to change the air’s direction, so there must be a reaction.
notes.evidence: As the air travels around a wing and leaves the trailing edge, the air is forced to move in a downward direction. Since a force is required to make something change direction, there must be an equal and opposite reacting force. In this case, the reacting force is what we call lift.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Lift and Newton’s Third Law”, p. 5-37

notes.front: What is the Doppler effect for sound from a moving aeroplane?
notes.back: Its motion raises the frequency sensed ahead of it and lowers the frequency sensed behind it.
notes.explanation: It explains why an aeroplane sounds different approaching than when it is overhead.
notes.evidence: the object’s forward motion adds to the frequency as sensed from the front and takes away from the frequency as sensed from the rear. This change in frequency is known as the Doppler Effect, and it explains why the sound from an airplane seems different as it approaches compared to how it sounds as it flies overhead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Doppler Effect”, p. 5-32

notes.front: Which two properties of a medium govern the velocity of sound in it?
notes.back: Density and elasticity.
notes.explanation: Even in one medium, the velocity varies with conditions such as temperature and pressure.
notes.evidence: Even in the same medium under different conditions of temperature, pressure, and so forth, the velocity of sound varies. Density and elasticity of a medium are the two basic physical properties which govern the velocity of sound.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Speed of Sound”, p. 5-31

notes.front: Where the speed of sound is 761 mph, what Mach number is an aircraft flying at 571 mph?
notes.choicesExplained: B divides the speed of sound by the aircraft’s speed. C subtracts. D slips the decimal point.
notes.explanation: Divide the aircraft’s speed by the local speed of sound: 571 ÷ 761 ≈ 0.75.
notes.evidence: If the speed of sound at sea level is 761 mph, an aircraft flying at a Mach number of 1.2 at sea level would be traveling at a speed of 761 mph × 1.2 = 913 mph.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Mach Number”, p. 5-31

notes.front: Why is the speed of sound lower at 30,000 ft than at sea level in the standard atmosphere?
notes.back: C: The air is colder
notes.choices:
A) The air is less dense, which slows sound
B) Gravity is weaker
C) The air is colder
D) The air is more humid
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are not the cause the handbook gives: the speed of sound in air follows temperature.
notes.explanation: The speed of sound in air increases as temperature increases, so colder air at altitude carries it more slowly.
notes.evidence: of sound in air changes with temperature, increasing as temperature increases. Figure 5-75 shows how the speed of sound changes with altitude.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “The Speed of Sound”, p. 5-47

notes.front: What is the critical Mach number, and what range is typically transonic?
notes.back: The speed at which the shock wave forms; transonic is typically Mach 0.80 to 1.20.
notes.explanation: It marks the speed at which the shock wave first appears.
notes.evidence: The speed at which the shock wave forms is known as the critical Mach number. Transonic speed is typically between Mach 0.80 and 1.20.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Subsonic, Transonic, and Supersonic Flight”, p. 5-47

notes.front: Part of an aeroplane has subsonic airflow and part has supersonic airflow. Which flight regime is it in?
notes.back: C: Transonic
notes.choices:
A) Subsonic
B) Supersonic
C) Transonic
D) Hypersonic
notes.choicesExplained: A has all airflow below Mach 1. B has supersonic airflow over the entire aeroplane. D is faster than Mach 5.
notes.explanation: Transonic flight is defined by this mix of subsonic and supersonic airflow.
notes.evidence: When an airplane is flying at transonic speed, part of the airplane is experiencing subsonic airflow and part is experiencing supersonic airflow.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Subsonic, Transonic, and Supersonic Flight”, p. 5-47

notes.front: What can the normal shock wave on a wing do in transonic flight?
notes.back: Separate the airflow from the wing, and shift the centre of lift aft so the nose pitches down.
notes.explanation: These effects are why stability problems can arise in transonic flight.
notes.evidence: Stability problems can be encountered during transonic flight, because the shock wave can cause the airflow to separate from the wing. The shock wave also causes the center of lift to shift aft, causing the nose to pitch down.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Subsonic, Transonic, and Supersonic Flight”, p. 5-47

notes.front: What is the air like behind a normal shock wave?
notes.back: Subsonic, with higher static pressure and density.
notes.explanation: Normal shock waves form perpendicular to the airstream.
notes.evidence: Normal shock waves form perpendicular to the airstream. The velocity of the air behind a normal shock wave is subsonic, and the static pressure and density of the air are higher.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Normal Shock Wave”, p. 5-48

notes.front: Where is the aerodynamic centre of a subsonic aerofoil, and where does it move in supersonic flight?
notes.back: About 25 percent of the chord back from the leading edge; it moves back to 50 percent.
notes.explanation: The move causes significant changes in the aeroplane’s control and stability.
notes.evidence: For a subsonic airfoil, the aerodynamic center, or the point of support, is approximately 25 percent of the way back from the wing leading edge. In supersonic flight, the aerodynamic center moves back to 50 percent of the wing’s chord, causing some significant changes in the airplane’s control and stability.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “High-Speed Airfoils”, p. 5-48

notes.front: Why was the Blackbird, cruising at Mach 3.5, built of titanium alloy rather than aluminium alloy?
notes.back: To withstand aerodynamic heating: skin temperatures from 450 °F to over 1,000 °F.
notes.explanation: Aluminium alloy was the traditional material that the high temperatures ruled out.
notes.evidence: When the SR-71 Blackbird airplane is cruising at Mach 3.5, skin temperatures on its surface range from 450 °F to over 1,000 °F. To withstand this high temperature, the airplane was constructed of titanium alloy, instead of the traditional aluminum alloy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Aerodynamic Heating”, p. 5-49

notes.front: At about what heights is the air too thin for respiration, and too short of oxygen for combustion?
notes.back: About 6 miles for respiration; about 12 miles for combustion, except in some specially designed turbine aeroplanes.
notes.explanation: The air’s composition stays almost constant with height, but its density diminishes rapidly.
notes.evidence: The composition of the air remains almost constant from sea level up to its highest level, but its density diminishes rapidly with altitude. Six miles up, for example, it is too thin to support respiration, and 12 miles up, there is not enough oxygen to support combustion, except in some specially designed turbine engine powered airplanes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Composition of the Atmosphere”, p. 5-33

notes.front: In which layer of the atmosphere are nearly all cloud formations and generally turbulent conditions found?
notes.back: D: The troposphere
notes.choices:
A) The exosphere
B) The stratosphere
C) The ionosphere
D) The troposphere
notes.choicesExplained: B lies above the tropopause. C is marked by ions and free electrons. A is the outer layer, beginning at 600 miles.
notes.explanation: The troposphere is marked by large changes in temperature and humidity.
notes.evidence: The troposphere is characterized by large changes in temperature and humidity and by generally turbulent conditions. Nearly all cloud formations are within the troposphere.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Composition of the Atmosphere”, p. 5-33

notes.front: Why is atmospheric pressure lower at 8,000 ft than at 5,000 ft?
notes.back: B: Less weight of air lies above the higher point
notes.choices:
A) Colder air weighs more, so pressure falls
B) Less weight of air lies above the higher point
C) Gravity is stronger higher up
D) Humidity rises with height
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are not the cause the handbook gives.
notes.explanation: Atmospheric pressure at any altitude comes from the weight of air above it, which is less higher up.
notes.evidence: Since atmospheric pressure at any altitude is due to the weight of air above it, pressure decreases with increased altitude.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Atmospheric Pressure”, p. 5-34

notes.front: Standard sea level conditions are a pressure of 29.92 inches of mercury and a temperature of {{c1::15 °C (59 °F)}}.
notes.explanation: Standard gravity at sea level is taken as 32.174 fps/s.
notes.evidence: The standard sea level conditions are: Pressure at 0 altitude (P0) = 29.92 "Hg Temperature at 0 altitude (T0) = 15 °C or 59 °F Gravity at 0 altitude (G0) = 32.174 fps/s
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Standard Atmosphere”, p. 5-36

notes.front: Two flight tests of the same aeroplane, on a hot day and a cold one, give different takeoff results. What must be done before the results are compared?
notes.back: A: Refer both to a standard reference condition
notes.choices:
A) Refer both to a standard reference condition
B) Repeat the tests until the weather matches
C) Average the two days’ readings
D) Discard the hotter day’s results
notes.choicesExplained: C and D do not remove the effect of the conditions. B is not practical: conditions are rarely the same twice.
notes.explanation: A standard reference condition has to be set first before performance results can be compared.
notes.evidence: If the performance of an aircraft is computed, either through flight tests or wind tunnel tests, some standard reference condition must be determined first in order to compare results
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Standard Atmosphere”, p. 5-36

notes.front: Density altitude is a calculated altitude obtained by correcting {{c1::pressure altitude}} for temperature.
notes.explanation: Actual altitude and density altitude can differ, as when air at 12,000 ft has the standard density for 10,000 ft.
notes.evidence: In this case, at an actual altitude of 12,000 ft, we have air that has the same density as standard air at 10,000 ft. Density altitude is a calculated altitude obtained by correcting pressure altitude for temperature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Atmospheric Density”, p. 5-34

notes.front: On a cold day of high pressure, the air density that is standard for 8,000 ft is found at 9,500 ft. An aeroplane is at 9,500 ft. What is the density altitude?
notes.choicesExplained: A is the true altitude, which density altitude need not equal. D adds the altitudes. C is their difference.
notes.explanation: Density altitude is the altitude whose standard density matches the air actually present.
notes.evidence: For example, on a day when the atmospheric pressure is higher than standard and the temperature is lower than standard, the density which is standard at 10,000 ft might occur at 12,000 ft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Atmospheric Density”, p. 5-34

notes.front: How is allowable takeoff gross weight generally treated in consistently humid areas, and why?
notes.back: It is generally reduced, because humid air is less dense than dry air.
notes.explanation: Humidity has important effects during takeoff, though at cruise power they are small.
notes.evidence: During takeoff, however, humidity has important effects. Two things are done to compensate for the effects of humidity on takeoff performance. Since humid air is less dense than dry air, the allowable takeoff gross weight of an aircraft is generally reduced for operation in areas that are consistently humid.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Water Content of the Atmosphere”, p. 5-34

notes.front: A piston aeroplane is to take off on a hot, very humid day. What should the mechanic expect of the engine?
notes.back: D: Less power output than in dry air
notes.choices:
A) Less power only at cruise, not at takeoff
B) More power, because moist air is denser
C) No change, since fuel is metered by weight
D) Less power output than in dry air
notes.choicesExplained: B has density backwards: humid air is less dense. C ignores that water vapour does not burn. A reverses when the effect matters.
notes.explanation: Humidity decreases a reciprocating engine’s power output, so manifold pressure may need raising.
notes.evidence: Second, because the power output of reciprocating engines is decreased by humidity, the manifold pressure may need to be increased above that recommended for takeoff in dry air in order to obtain the same power output.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Water Content of the Atmosphere”, p. 5-35

notes.front: Air cools overnight while its absolute humidity stays the same. What happens to its relative humidity?
notes.back: C: It rises
notes.choices:
A) It falls
B) It stays the same
C) It rises
D) It drops to zero
notes.choicesExplained: A and D have it backwards. B confuses relative with absolute humidity, which is what stays the same.
notes.explanation: Cooler air needs less water vapour to become saturated, so the same vapour is a larger share.
notes.evidence: If the temperature drops and the absolute humidity remain constant, the relative humidity will increase. This is because less water vapor is required to saturate the air at the lower temperature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Relative Humidity”, p. 5-36

notes.front: A chilled metal part brought from a cold store into a warm, humid hangar quickly becomes wet on its surface. Why?
notes.back: A: Air touching the part is cooled below its dew point
notes.choices:
A) Air touching the part is cooled below its dew point
B) The hangar’s air pressure is higher
C) The metal releases water it absorbed in the cold
D) Water evaporates from the part
notes.choicesExplained: C is not how metal behaves. B is not the cause. D is the opposite of what is happening.
notes.explanation: When air is cooled below its dew point, some of its water vapour condenses out.
notes.evidence: The air immediately in contact with the glasses was cooled below its dew point temperature, and some of the water vapor was condensed out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Dew Point”, p. 5-36

notes.front: What are the four forces acting on an aeroplane in flight?
notes.back: Lift, weight, thrust and drag.
notes.explanation: Drag is the friction of the air flowing around the aeroplane.
notes.evidence: These forces are lift, weight, thrust, and drag. [Figure 5-53] Lift is the upward force created by the wing, weight is the pull of gravity on the mass, thrust is the force created by the airplane’s propeller or turbine engine, and drag is the friction caused by the air flowing around the airplane.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Four Forces of Flight”, p. 5-36

notes.front: An aeroplane is flying at a constant velocity. How do its thrust and drag compare?
notes.back: D: Thrust and drag are equal
notes.choices:
A) Thrust is greater than drag
B) Thrust is less than drag
C) Drag has fallen to zero
D) Thrust and drag are equal
notes.choicesExplained: A describes accelerating. B describes decelerating. C never happens while air flows around the aeroplane.
notes.explanation: Unbalanced forces mean something is changing; at constant velocity thrust and drag balance.
notes.evidence: When an airplane is accelerating, it has more thrust than drag. 2. When an airplane is decelerating, it has less thrust than drag. 3. When an airplane is at a constant velocity, thrust and drag are equal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Four Forces of Flight”, p. 5-36

notes.front: An aeroplane is climbing. How do its lift and weight compare?
notes.back: A: Lift is greater than weight
notes.choices:
A) Lift is greater than weight
B) Weight is greater than lift
C) Lift and weight are equal
D) Lift has no bearing on climb
notes.choicesExplained: B describes descending. C describes constant altitude. D ignores the vertical balance of forces.
notes.explanation: Lift exceeding weight is the condition the handbook gives for a climb.
notes.evidence: When an airplane is climbing, it has more lift than weight. 5. When an airplane is descending, it has more weight than lift. 6. When an airplane is at a constant altitude, lift and weight are equal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Four Forces of Flight”, p. 5-37

notes.front: What gives a wing a high aspect ratio, and what does a higher aspect ratio produce?
notes.back: A long span with a very narrow chord; less drag for a given flight speed.
notes.explanation: Such wings are typically found on glider-type aircraft.
notes.evidence: If a wing has a long span and a very narrow chord, it is said to have a high aspect ratio. A higher aspect ratio produces less drag for a given flight speed, and is typically found on glider type aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Airfoils”, p. 5-39

notes.front: Why keep a wing’s surface smooth and clean?
notes.back: It delays the onset of a stall, letting the wing operate at a higher angle of attack.
notes.explanation: Ice on a wing is serious partly because of its effect on boundary layer air.
notes.evidence: With a smooth and clean wing surface, the onset of a stall is delayed and the wing can operate at a higher angle of attack. One of the reasons ice forming on a wing can be such a serious problem is because of its effect on boundary layer air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Boundary Layer Control”, p. 5-39

notes.front: On what aeroplanes are vortex generators used, and what problem do they address?
notes.back: Aeroplanes flying at high subsonic speed, where a shock wave on the wing makes the air separate.
notes.explanation: The shock wave forms on top of the wing when the air there reaches Mach 1.
notes.evidence: Vortex generators are used on airplanes that fly at high subsonic speed, where the velocity of the air on the top of the wing can reach Mach 1. As the air reaches Mach 1 velocity, a shock wave forms on the top of the wing, and the subsequent shock wave causes the air to separate from the wing’s upper surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Boundary Layer Control”, p. 5-40

notes.front: During a wing repair on a high subsonic jet, a mechanic finds short aerofoils fixed in pairs on the upper surface. What are they for?
notes.back: B: Pulling high-energy air into the boundary layer to prevent separation
notes.choices:
A) Adding weight ahead of the hinge line
B) Pulling high-energy air into the boundary layer to prevent separation
C) Holding the ailerons in a deflected position
D) Increasing the wing’s camber for landing
notes.choicesExplained: A describes balance weights on control surfaces. C describes trim tabs. D describes flaps.
notes.explanation: These are vortex generators, placed to feed energetic air into the boundary layer.
notes.evidence: They are positioned such that they pull high-energy air down into the boundary layer region and prevent airflow separation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Boundary Layer Control”, p. 5-40

notes.front: Besides vortex generators, which additional aerodynamic devices does the ACS name in its physics element?
notes.back: Wing fences and stall strips.
notes.explanation: The ACS lists all three as additional aerodynamic devices a mechanic must know.
notes.evidence: AM.I.J.K11 Additional aerodynamic devices, including vortex generators, wing fences, and stall strips.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), I.J Physics for Aviation, Area I, Task J, Knowledge, p. 16

notes.front: Where do an aeroplane’s three axes of rotation intersect?
notes.back: At the centre of gravity.
notes.explanation: Pivoting on any one axis is, in essence, pivoting around the centre of gravity.
notes.evidence: These axes of rotation are the longitudinal, lateral, and vertical. On the airplane, all three axes intersect at the center of gravity. As the airplane pivots on one of these axes, it is in essence pivoting around the center of gravity (CG).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Axes of an Aircraft”, p. 5-40

notes.front: Movement around the vertical axis is called what, and which control produces it?
notes.back: Yaw, produced by the rudder.
notes.explanation: Control around this axis is called directional control.
notes.evidence: The vertical axis of an airplane runs from top to bottom through the middle of the airplane, passing through the center of gravity. Movement around this axis is known as yaw, and control around this axis is called directional control. Movement around this axis is controlled by the rudder
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flight Controls and the Vertical Axis”, p. 5-43

notes.front: Movement around the lateral axis is called what, and which control usually produces it?
notes.back: Pitch, usually produced by the elevator.
notes.explanation: Control around this wingtip-to-wingtip axis is called longitudinal control.
notes.evidence: The lateral axis of an airplane is a line that runs below the wing, from wingtip to wingtip, passing through the airplane’s center of gravity. Movement around this axis is called pitch, and control around this axis is called longitudinal control. The flight control that handles this job is the elevator
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flight Controls & the Lateral Axis”, p. 5-42

notes.front: Movement around the longitudinal axis is called what, and which controls produce it?
notes.back: Roll, produced by the ailerons, aided on jet transports by spoilers.
notes.explanation: Control around it is called lateral control.
notes.evidence: Movement around this axis is known as roll, and control around this axis is called lateral control. Movement around this axis is controlled by the ailerons, and on jet transport airplanes, it is aided by surfaces on the wing known as spoilers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flight Controls and the Longitudinal Axis”, p. 5-43

notes.front: A pilot turns the control wheel to the right. What do the ailerons do?
notes.back: B: The right aileron rises and the left one lowers
notes.choices:
A) Both ailerons rise
B) The right aileron rises and the left one lowers
C) The left aileron rises and the right one lowers
D) Both ailerons lower
notes.choicesExplained: A and D would change lift on both wings alike, giving no roll. C is a left turn.
notes.explanation: The raised right aileron reduces that wing’s lift; the left wing gains lift, and with it induced drag that yaws the nose left.
notes.evidence: We start by turning the control wheel to the right, which raises the right aileron and lowers the left aileron and initiates the banking turn. The increased lift on the left wing also increases the induced drag on the left wing, which tries to make the nose of the airplane yaw to the left.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flight Controls and the Vertical Axis”, p. 5-44

notes.front: What is a stabilator, and what does it do when the pilot pulls back on the control wheel?
notes.back: A fully moving horizontal surface for pitch control; the whole surface moves, trailing edge up.
notes.explanation: Unlike an elevator, the entire horizontal surface moves.
notes.evidence: On the Piper Cherokee Cruiser PA-28-140 shown in Figure 5-66, pulling back on the control wheel causes the entire horizontal surface, or stabilator, to move, with the trailing edge deflecting upward.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flight Controls & the Lateral Axis”, p. 5-43

notes.front: What is an aeroplane’s static stability, and what does positive static stability mean?
notes.back: Its initial response once its equilibrium is disrupted; positive means it tends to return to its original position.
notes.explanation: Static stability describes only the first reaction after the disruptive force is removed.
notes.evidence: The initial response that an airplane displays after its equilibrium is disrupted is referred to as its static stability. If the static stability is positive, the airplane will tend to return to its original position after the disruptive force is removed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Static Stability”, p. 5-40

notes.front: A gust yaws an aeroplane’s nose to the left. After the gust, the nose stays at its new heading and moves no further. How is its static stability described?
notes.back: C: Neutral
notes.choices:
A) Positive
B) Negative
C) Neutral
D) Positive static with negative dynamic stability
notes.choicesExplained: A would return the nose. B would keep it moving further away. D describes oscillations, not the initial response.
notes.explanation: Remaining displaced without moving toward greater displacement is neutral static stability.
notes.evidence: If an airplane tends to remain in a displaced position after the force is removed, but does not continue to move toward even greater displacement, its static stability is described as being neutral.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Static Stability”, p. 5-40

notes.front: After a disturbance, an aeroplane’s nose oscillates up and down, and each swing is larger than the one before. How is its dynamic stability classified?
notes.back: D: Negative
notes.choices:
A) Neutral static stability
B) Positive
C) Neutral
D) Negative
notes.choicesExplained: B would have oscillations that lessen. C would have oscillations that stay the same. A concerns the initial response, not the oscillations.
notes.explanation: Oscillations that increase over time mean negative dynamic stability.
notes.evidence: If the oscillations lessen over time, the airplane is still classified as having positive dynamic stability. If the oscillations increase over time, the airplane is classified as having negative dynamic stability. If the oscillations remain the same over time, the airplane is classified as having neutral dynamic stability.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Dynamic Stability”, p. 5-41

notes.front: For good longitudinal stability, where is the centre of gravity typically placed, and what balances the result?
notes.back: Forward of the centre of lift; the nose-down tendency is balanced by the horizontal stabiliser and elevator.
notes.explanation: The forward placement gives a nose-down pitching tendency that the tail must counter.
notes.evidence: For an airplane to have good longitudinal stability, the center of gravity is typically located forward of the center of lift. This gives the airplane a nosedown pitching tendency, which is balanced out by the force generated at the horizontal stabilizer and elevator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Longitudinal Stability”, p. 5-41

notes.front: An aeroplane is loaded with its centre of gravity behind the aft limit. What tendency does the handbook warn of?
notes.back: B: A nose-up pitch that can lead to a stall and loss of control
notes.choices:
A) A nose-down pitch the tail cannot counter
B) A nose-up pitch that can lead to a stall and loss of control
C) A Dutch roll
D) No change, as long as the weight is within limits
notes.choicesExplained: A is the risk of a centre of gravity too far forward. C arises from dihedral and fin effects in a slip. D ignores the centre of gravity limits.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls a centre of gravity behind the aft limit especially dangerous.
notes.evidence: It is especially dangerous if the center of gravity is behind the aft limit. The airplane will now have a tendency to pitch noseup, which can lead to the wing stalling and possible loss of control of the airplane.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Longitudinal Stability”, p. 5-42

notes.front: What is dihedral, and what does it tend to give an aeroplane?
notes.back: An upward wing angle from the horizontal, usually a few degrees; it tends to give good lateral stability.
notes.explanation: It is a design characteristic built into the wing.
notes.evidence: One design characteristic that tends to give an airplane good lateral stability is called dihedral. Dihedral is an upward wing angle, with respect to the horizontal, and it is usually just a few degrees.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Lateral Stability”, p. 5-42

notes.front: The right wing of a low-wing aeroplane with a few degrees of dihedral drops in turbulence. How does dihedral bring it back to level?
notes.back: C: A sideslip toward the low wing raises its angle of attack and lift
notes.choices:
A) The raised left wing gains angle of attack and lifts further
B) The rudder deflects automatically
C) A sideslip toward the low wing raises its angle of attack and lift
D) The centre of gravity shifts toward the high wing
notes.choicesExplained: A has the wings reversed. B describes nothing dihedral does. D does not happen in flight.
notes.explanation: The sideslip toward the low wing increases its angle of attack, and the extra lift raises it back to level.
notes.evidence: When the left wing drops, this will cause the airplane to experience a sideslip toward the low wing. The sideslip causes the low wing to experience a higher angle of attack, which increases its lift and raises it back to a level flight attitude.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Lateral Stability”, p. 5-42

notes.front: A gust swings an aeroplane’s nose to the left. Which part tends to realign it with the relative wind?
notes.back: C: The vertical fin
notes.choices:
A) The ailerons
B) The wing dihedral
C) The vertical fin
D) The elevator trim tab
notes.choicesExplained: A controls roll. B gives lateral stability, not directional. D holds the elevator deflected for pitch.
notes.explanation: The vertical fin provides directional stability, aligning the aeroplane with the relative wind.
notes.evidence: The vertical fin gives the airplane this stability, causing the airplane to align with the relative wind.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Directional Stability”, p. 5-42

notes.front: Which way does an anti-servo tab on a stabilator move, and what does it achieve?
notes.back: The same way as the trailing edge, creating a force against the movement that reduces sensitivity to pilot input.
notes.explanation: Its force acts against the stabilator’s own movement.
notes.evidence: As the trailing edge of the stabilator moves down, the anti-servo tab moves down and creates a force trying to raise the trailing edge. With this force acting against the movement of the stabilator, it reduces the sensitivity to pilot input.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Anti-servo Tab”, p. 5-44

notes.front: Which way does a balance tab move, and what does it do?
notes.back: Opposite to the flight control’s trailing edge, producing a force that helps the control move.
notes.explanation: It works in just the opposite way to an anti-servo tab.
notes.evidence: In these cases, a balance tab can be used to generate a force that assists in the movement of the flight control. Just the opposite of anti-servo tabs, balance tabs move in the opposite direction of the flight control’s trailing edge, providing a force that helps the flight control move.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Balance Tab”, p. 5-44

notes.front: What do the servo tabs on a Boeing 727 do?
notes.back: Back up the hydraulic system if it fails; in normal flight they act like balance tabs.
notes.explanation: Like a balance tab, a servo tab moves opposite to the control’s trailing edge.
notes.evidence: Like the balance tab, the servo tab moves in the opposite direction of the flight control’s trailing edge. The Boeing 727 has servo tabs that back up the hydraulic system in the event of a failure. During normal flight, the servo tabs act like balance tabs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Servo Tab”, p. 5-45

notes.front: A pilot adjusts a small surface from the flight deck so the elevator stays slightly deflected without anyone holding the control wheel. Which tab is it?
notes.back: C: A trim tab
notes.choices:
A) An anti-servo tab
B) A balance tab
C) A trim tab
D) A servo tab
notes.choicesExplained: B only assists control movement. A resists movement to reduce sensitivity. D moves the control when hydraulics fail.
notes.explanation: A trim tab creates a force that keeps the flight control deflected, relieving the pilot.
notes.evidence: To relieve the pilot of the need to hold back pressure on the control wheel, a trim tab on the elevator can be adjusted to hold the elevator in a slightly deflected position.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Tabs, Trim Tabs”, p. 5-44

notes.front: What do flaps do to a wing, and where can they be installed?
notes.back: They change its camber, increasing lift and drag at any angle of attack; they fit on the trailing edge, or leading edge on larger aeroplanes.
notes.explanation: The handbook names four types in use: plain, split, slotted and Fowler.
notes.evidence: Flaps can be installed on the leading edge or trailing edge, with the leading edge versions used only on larger airplanes. Flaps change the camber of the wing, and they increase both the lift and the drag for any given angle of attack. The four different types of flaps in use are called the plain, split, slotted, and Fowler.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flaps”, p. 5-45

notes.front: What does a plain flap do when it is lowered?
notes.back: It increases the wing’s effective camber and chord line, giving more lift and more drag.
notes.explanation: It sits on the trailing edge, inboard of the ailerons, and forms part of the wing surface.
notes.evidence: Plain flaps attach to the trailing edge of the wing, inboard of the ailerons, and form part of the wing’s overall surface. When deployed downward, they increase the effective camber of the wing and the wing’s chord line. Both of these factors cause the wing to create more lift and more drag.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flaps”, p. 5-45

notes.front: How does a split flap deploy, and how does its drag compare with a plain flap’s?
notes.back: Downward from the bottom of the wing, leaving the top surface unchanged; it makes more drag, from extra turbulence.
notes.explanation: Because the top surface stays as it was, only the underside changes shape.
notes.evidence: The split flap attaches to the bottom of the wing, and deploys downward without changing the top surface of the wing. This type of flap creates more drag than the plain flap because of the increase in turbulence.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flaps”, p. 5-45

notes.front: How does a slotted flap produce additional lift?
notes.back: Its leading edge drops slightly, opening a slot that lets high-pressure air from under the wing flow over the flap.
notes.explanation: The added airflow over the top of the flap is the source of the extra lift.
notes.evidence: By having the leading edge drop down slightly, a slot opens, which lets some of the high-pressure air on the bottom of the wing flow over the top of the flap. This additional airflow over the top of the flap produces additional lift.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flaps”, p. 5-45

notes.front: A flap runs aft on a track and roller system as it lowers, increasing the total wing area as well as camber and chord line. Which type is it?
notes.back: D: Fowler flap
notes.choices:
A) Plain flap
B) Slotted flap
C) Split flap
D) Fowler flap
notes.choicesExplained: A only hinges down from the trailing edge. C drops from the underside. B drops its leading edge to open a slot, without moving aft on tracks.
notes.explanation: The Fowler flap is the most effective of the four types.
notes.evidence: The Fowler flap attaches to the back of the wing using a track and roller system. When it deploys, it moves aft in addition to deflecting downward. This increases the total wing area, in addition to increasing the wing camber and chord line. This type of flap is the most effective of the four types
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Flaps”, p. 5-45

notes.front: How do leading edge slats differ from leading edge slots?
notes.back: Slats serve the same purpose but are movable and can be retracted when not needed.
notes.explanation: On some aeroplanes, slats have deployed automatically in response to aerodynamic forces at high angle of attack.
notes.evidence: Leading edge slats serve the same purpose as slots, the difference being that slats are movable and can be retracted when not needed. On some airplanes, leading edge slats have been automatic in operation, deploying in response to the aerodynamic forces that come into play during a high angle of attack.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Leading Edge Slats”, p. 5-46

notes.front: A wing is built with a greater angle of incidence at the root than at the tip. What is this called, and what does it achieve?
notes.back: C: Washout; the inboard wing stalls first, keeping aileron control
notes.choices:
A) Dihedral; it gives lateral stability
B) Camber; it increases lift at the tip
C) Washout; the inboard wing stalls first, keeping aileron control
D) Sweepback; it delays the shock wave
notes.choicesExplained: A is an upward wing angle, not a change of incidence. B is surface curvature. D is a planform for high subsonic speed.
notes.explanation: With washout, the outboard part of the wing, where the ailerons are, keeps flying as the stall begins.
notes.evidence: Many airplanes are designed with a greater angle of incidence at the root of the wing than at the tip, and this is referred to as washout. This feature causes the inboard part of the wing to stall before the outboard part, which helps maintain aileron control during the initial stages of a wing stall.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Airfoils”, p. 5-39

notes.front: What is dissymmetry of lift in a helicopter’s forward flight?
notes.back: The advancing blade meets faster airflow and makes more lift than the retreating blade.
notes.explanation: Left unchecked, the extra lift would roll the helicopter and lead to a crash.
notes.evidence: The advancing blade is moving toward the relative wind, and therefore experiences a greater velocity of airflow. The increased lift created by the blade on the right side will try to roll the helicopter to the left. If this condition is allowed to exist, it will ultimately lead to the helicopter crashing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Forward Flight”, p. 5-55

notes.front: How does a helicopter’s tail rotor counteract the main rotor’s torque?
notes.back: Its thrust in pounds times its distance from the main rotor in feet gives an opposing torque in pound-feet.
notes.explanation: Torque is force acting along a distance, here the distance between the two rotors.
notes.evidence: The tail rotor force, in pounds, multiplied by the distance from the tail rotor to the main rotor, in feet, creates a torque in pound-feet that counteracts the main rotor torque.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Anti-Torque Systems”, p. 5-50

notes.front: What is autorotation?
notes.back: A flight condition where the main rotor is driven by the relative wind passing through the blades, not by the engine.
notes.explanation: It is similar to an aeroplane gliding after its engine fails.
notes.evidence: Autorotation is a flight condition where the main rotor blades are driven by the force of the relative wind passing through the blades, rather than by the engine. This flight condition is similar to an airplane gliding if its engine fails while in
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Autorotation”, p. 5-56

notes.front: When about what share of a helicopter’s rotor system is stalled will control be lost?
notes.back: About 25 percent.
notes.explanation: High density altitude is among the conditions that lead to rotor blade stall.
notes.evidence: When approximately 25 percent of the rotor system is stalled, due to the problems with the advancing and retreating blades, control of the helicopter will be lost. Conditions that will lead to the rotor blades stalling include high forward speed, heavy gross weight, turbulent air, high-density altitude, and steep or abrupt turns.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Advancing Blade and Retreating Blade Problems”, p. 5-56

notes.front: How does a weight-shift control trike bank, compared with a conventional small aeroplane?
notes.back: Shifting weight twists the wing, changing its angle of attack; an aeroplane uses ailerons to alter camber.
notes.explanation: Either way, differential lift between the wings is what produces the bank.
notes.evidence: A traditional small airplane, like a Cessna 172, turns or banks by using the ailerons, effectively altering the camber of the wing and thereby generating differential lift. By comparison, weight shift on a trike actually causes the wing to twist, which changes the angle of attack on the wing and causes the differential lift to exist that banks the trike.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Weight-Shift Control, Flexible Wing Aircraft Aerodynamics”, p. 5-58

notes.front: How does a powered parachute pilot control climbing and descending?
notes.back: With engine power: advancing the throttle climbs, retarding it descends.
notes.explanation: The inflated wing makes a lot of drag, so reducing power gives a very controllable descent.
notes.evidence: Once the powered parachute is in flight, control over climbing and descending is handled with engine power. Advancing the throttle makes the aircraft climb, and retarding the throttle makes it descend. The inflated wing creates a lot of drag in flight, so reducing the engine power creates a very controllable descent of the aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 5, “Powered Parachute Aerodynamics”, p. 5-59

notes.front: When repairing or refinishing a control surface, what must a repair not add, and why?
notes.back: Weight aft of the hinge line, which may upset the surface’s balance enough to induce flutter.
notes.explanation: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B stresses this especially for high performance aeroplanes.
notes.evidence: When repairing or refinishing control surfaces, especially on high performance airplanes, care must be exercised that the repairs do not involve the addition of weight aft of the hinge line. Such a procedure may adversely affect the balance of the surface to a degree that could induce flutter.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), Chapter 1, Section 3, para 1-38 “Control Surface Flutter Precautions”, p. 1-16

notes.front: After refinishing a balanced aileron, a painter proposes two extra coats beyond the manufacturer’s scheme for durability. What does Advisory Circular 43.13-1B say?
notes.back: C: Avoid coats beyond what the manufacturer originally applied
notes.choices:
A) Extra coats are fine if the aileron stays under its maximum weight
B) Extra coats are fine if balance weight is added aft of the hinge
C) Avoid coats beyond what the manufacturer originally applied
D) Only the colour scheme matters
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that balance, not just weight, is at stake. B adds weight on the wrong side of the hinge. D ignores the circular’s special emphasis on paint.
notes.explanation: Too many extra coats of paint on balanced control surfaces get special emphasis in the circular.
notes.evidence: Special emphasis is directed to the effect of too many extra coats of paint on balanced control surfaces. Mechanics must avoid adding additional coats of paint in excess of what the manufacturer originally applied.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), Chapter 4, Section 3, para 4-36 “Flutter and Vibration Precautions”, p. 4-12

notes.front: A repaired elevator now hangs tail-heavy about its hinge. Per Advisory Circular 43.13-1B, how may balance be restored?
notes.back: B: Counter-balance weight forward of the hinge line, per the manufacturer’s instructions, then flight test
notes.choices:
A) Weight aft of the hinge line, at the mechanic’s judgement
B) Counter-balance weight forward of the hinge line, per the manufacturer’s instructions, then flight test
C) Any weight anywhere, provided the surface is repainted
D) Nothing may be done; the surface must be scrapped
notes.choicesExplained: A puts weight on the side that invites flutter and skips the manufacturer. C ignores where the weight goes. D is not what the circular says.
notes.explanation: Balance weights are added or removed only when necessary and per the manufacturer, and flight testing must confirm flutter is not a problem.
notes.evidence: Under certain conditions, counter-balance weight is added forward of the hinge line to maintain balance. Add or remove balance weights only when necessary in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Flight testing must be accomplished to ensure flutter is not a problem.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), Chapter 4, Section 3, para 4-36 “Flutter and Vibration Precautions”, p. 4-12
